---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:slope-stability}
The tower is slope stable if some $n_0\geq1$ satisfies, for all $n\geq n_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-strong-stability}
 S_n=
 \left(
 \bigsqcup_{j=0}^{p^{n-n_0}-1}
 \frac{j+(\{0\}\sqcup S_{n_0})}{p^{n-n_0}}
 \right)\setminus\{0\}.
\end{equation}
The final multiset operation removes one zero.  We also call this
strong slope stability to distinguish it from partial propagation.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:block-propagation}
For $1\leq b\leq p$, the first $b$ blocks are eventually stable if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:b-block-slopes}
 S_{n+1}\cap(0,b/p)
 =\bigsqcup_{j=0}^{b-1}\frac{j+S_n}{p}
 \ \sqcup\ \left\{\frac1p,\ldots,\frac{b-1}{p}\right\}
 \qquad(n\gg0).
\end{equation}
The final multiset is empty when $b=1$. The case $b=1$ is also called
complete first-block propagation.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{ques:first-block-count}
For a given tower, what is the largest $b\in\{0,1,\ldots,p\}$ for
which the first $b$ blocks are eventually stable? Here $b=0$ means
that even the first block is not eventually stable.
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:KZ-stability}
Assume eventual minimal break ratios. Then the tower is slope stable
provided that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-gap}
 \deg f_i\leq\delta p^i-C\qquad\text{for all sufficiently large }i,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:KZ-gap-constant}
 C=\frac{a(p-1)(d-1)^2}{8}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{ques:KZ-gap}
Can the degree-gap condition be removed?  Equivalently, can one take
$C=0$ in the sufficient condition: does every $\mathbf Z_p$-tower of $\mathbf P^1$,
ramified only at infinity and with eventual minimal break ratios,
have slope stability?
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
For every $p\geq5$, the tower defined by
\eqref{eq:main-witt-vector} is ramified
only at infinity and has
\[
 s_n=(p+1)p^{n-1},\qquad
 g_n=\frac{p^{2n}-p^n}{2}.
\]
It has minimal break ratios but is not slope stable.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:gap}
Under eventual minimal break ratios, the condition
$\deg f_i\leq\delta p^i$ does not imply slope stability.
For the parameters in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, even
$\deg f_i\leq\delta p^i-2$ for every $i\geq1$ is insufficient.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:partial-stability}\label{cor:left-interval}
Assume eventual minimal break ratios. For every $n>m$ satisfying
\[
 p^{n-m-1}>\left\lceil\frac{a(d-1)^2}{8d}\right\rceil,
\]
one has the exact multiset identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:left-interval}
 S_{n+1}\cap\left(0,\frac1p-
       \frac{\lceil a(d-1)^2/(8d)\rceil}{p^{n-m}}\right)
 =\left(\frac1pS_n\right)\cap\left(0,\frac1p-
       \frac{\lceil a(d-1)^2/(8d)\rceil}{p^{n-m}}\right).
\end{equation}
Each side contains exactly $D_n-A-1$ slopes, counted with multiplicity.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-left-interval}\label{cor:intro-fixed-left}
Under eventual minimal break ratios, there is an integer $n_0\geq1$ such that
for every $n>n_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:growing-left-intro}
 S_{n+1}\cap\left(0,\frac1p-\frac1{p^{n-n_0+1}}\right)
 =\left(\frac1pS_n\right)\cap
   \left(0,\frac1p-\frac1{p^{n-n_0+1}}\right).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every fixed $0<c<1/p$,
\[
 S_{n+1}\cap(0,c)=\left(\frac1pS_n\right)\cap(0,c)
 \qquad(n\gg0).
\]
Equivalently, for every fixed $0<c<1$,
\[
 S_{n+1}\cap(0,c/p)=\frac1p\bigl(S_n\cap(0,c)\bigr)
 \qquad(n\gg0).
\]
In particular,
$S_{n+1}\cap(0,c)\supseteq\frac1p\bigl(S_n\cap(0,c)\bigr)$.
Here $c$ cuts off the source slopes before division by $p$; the
starting level may depend on $c$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-block-obstructions}
The following towers have minimal break ratios.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item Over $\mathbf F_7$, for
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-tower}
 f=[X]^{11}+\sum_{j\geq2}7^j[X]^{11\cdot7^j-19},
\end{equation}
complete first-block propagation fails at every $n\geq2$:
\[
 S_{n+1}\cap\left(0,\frac{1}{7}\right)\ne\frac17 S_n.
\]
\item Over $\mathbf F_5$, for
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-not-strong-tower}
 f=[X]^6+\sum_{j\geq1}5^j[X]^{6\cdot5^j-2},
\end{equation}
the first block propagates completely at every $n\geq2$:
\[
 S_{n+1}\cap\left(0,\frac{1}{5}\right)=\frac15 S_n.
\]
However, the two-block identity fails at every such level:
\[
 S_{n+1}\cap\left(0,\frac{2}{5}\right)
 \ne \frac15S_n\ \sqcup\ \frac{1+S_n}{5}\ \sqcup\ \left\{\frac{1}{5}\right\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
\label{ques:constant-field-degree}
Under the same minimal-break hypothesis, if the reduced defining Witt
vector $f$ is defined over $\mathbf F_q$ but need not descend to $\mathbf F_p$,
can the classical degree-gap constant, partial-stability loss, and
sufficient starting levels be chosen independently of $a$?
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-uniform}
Assume eventual minimal break ratios, with $\delta=d/p^m$ as above.
The following bounds hold over every $\mathbf F_q$ of characteristic $p$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item Recall that $D_n=dp^{n-m-1}$ for $n>m$. For every such $n$
satisfying
\[
 p^{n-m-1}>\frac{d+1}{8},
\]
one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-uniform-slopes}
 S_{n+1}\cap\left(0,\frac1p-
          \frac{\lfloor(d+1)/8\rfloor}{p^{n-m}}\right)
 =\left(\frac1pS_n\right)\cap\left(0,\frac1p-
          \frac{\lfloor(d+1)/8\rfloor}{p^{n-m}}\right).
\end{equation}
Each side contains exactly
\[
 d\left(p^{n-m-1}-\left\lfloor\frac{d+1}{8}\right\rfloor\right)-1
\]
slopes, counted with multiplicity.
\item The tower is slope stable provided that, for some integer $N>m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-uniform-degree-gap}
 \deg f_i\leq\delta p^i-C_{\mathrm u}\qquad(i\geq N),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-uniform-gap-constant}
 C_{\mathrm u}=\frac{p-1}{2}
                  \left\lfloor\frac{(d-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
A sufficient starting level depends only on $p,\delta,d,N$, and not
on $a$; an explicit formula is given in Theorem~\ref{thm:uniform-gap}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:geometric-tower}
A geometric $\mathbf Z_p$-tower over $\mathbf F_q$ is a sequence of finite
morphisms of smooth projective geometrically connected curves
\[
 \cdots\longrightarrow C_n\longrightarrow C_{n-1}\longrightarrow\cdots
 \longrightarrow C_0
\]
such that, on writing $K_n=\mathbf F_q(C_n)$ and
$K_\infty=\bigcup_nK_n$, the extension $K_\infty/K_0$ is Galois
with group $\mathbf Z_p$, the field $K_n$ is fixed by $p^n\mathbf Z_p$, and
$\mathbf F_q$ is algebraically closed in $K_\infty$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:reduced-equation}
The tower is defined by the Artin--Schreier--Witt equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:asw-equation}
 F(\mathbf y)-\mathbf y=f(X),
\end{equation}
where $F$ is Witt-vector Frobenius and $f$ has the reduced presentation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-witt}
 f=\sum_{i\geq0}p^i\sum_{\substack{\ell\geq1\\p\nmid\ell}}
       [a_{i,\ell}][X]^\ell,\qquad
 f_i(X)=\sum_{\substack{\ell\geq1\\p\nmid\ell}}a_{i,\ell}X^\ell
       \in\mathbf F_q[X],\qquad f_0\ne0.
\end{equation}
Here $[\cdot]$ denotes the Teichm\"uller lift, each $f_i$ is a
polynomial, and all displayed positive exponents are prime to $p$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:curve-zeta}
The zeta function of $C_n$ over $\mathbf F_q$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:curve-zeta}
 Z(C_n,s)=\exp\left(\sum_{r\geq1}
       \#C_n(\mathbf F_{q^r})\frac{s^r}{r}\right)
 =\frac{P(C_n,s)}{(1-s)(1-qs)},
\end{equation}
where $P(C_n,s)\in1+s\mathbf Z[s]$ has degree $2g(C_n)$.
Here $g(C_n)$ denotes the genus of $C_n$, and
$\#C_n(\mathbf F_{q^r})$ denotes the number of
$\mathbf F_{q^r}$-rational points on $C_n$.
The $q$-slopes of $C_n$ are the $v_q$-valuations of the reciprocal
roots of $P(C_n,s)$, counted with multiplicity, with $v_q(q)=1$.
They belong to $[0,1]$; the two denominator factors are not included.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:genus-stability}
Write $g_n=g(C_n)$.  The tower is genus stable if there are rational
constants $c_2,c_1,c_0$ such that
\[
 g_n=c_2p^{2n}+c_1p^n+c_0
 \qquad\text{for all sufficiently large }n.
\]
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Our $\mathbf Z_p$-tower is totally wildly ramified at infinity. As the genus
formula below shows, $g_n$ is bounded below by a quadratic polynomial
in $p^n$ with positive leading coefficient. Quadratic growth in $p^n$
is therefore the slowest possible growth, reflecting the mildest
possible asymptotic growth of wild ramification in this setting.
Genus stability requires this minimal growth rate to be realized by
an exact quadratic polynomial for all sufficiently large $n$.
In particular, the coefficient $c_2$ in
Definition~\ref{def:genus-stability} is necessarily positive.
Such geometric stability provides a natural starting point for seeking
stronger arithmetic regularity, especially stability of Newton slopes.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:conductors}
For a character $\chi_n$ of exact order $p^n$, let $s_n$ be its
largest upper ramification break at infinity, equivalently its
Swan conductor.  Its local Artin conductor exponent is $s_n+1$.
The order $p^n$ is also called the character conductor in the
slope-stability literature; it is distinct from these local
ramification conductors.  We use $s_n$ for the upper break
throughout.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:ramification-stability}
The upper breaks are ramification stable if
\[
 s_n=\lambda p^{n-1}+\mu\qquad(n\gg0)
\]
for fixed rational numbers $\lambda>0$ and $\mu$.
The break formula in Proposition~\ref{prop:KW-formulas} gives
\[
 s_{n+1}=\max\{ps_n,\deg f_n\}\geq ps_n.
\]
Substitution of the displayed expression for $s_n$, at two consecutive
sufficiently large levels, yields
$0\leq s_{n+1}-ps_n=(1-p)\mu$, and hence $\mu\leq0$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:KW-formulas}
For our $\mathbf Z_p$-tower, with reduced defining Witt vector $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-break-formula}
 s_n=\max_{0\leq i<n}p^{n-1-i}\deg f_i,\qquad \deg0=-\infty,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-genus-formula}
 2g_n=\sum_{r=1}^n(p-1)p^{r-1}(s_r-1).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The break formula \eqref{eq:intro-break-formula} is the specialization
of the ramification formula in \cite{KostersWan2018} to our tower,
ramified only at infinity.
There are $(p-1)p^{r-1}$ characters of exact order $p^r$,
each with local Artin conductor exponent $s_r+1$.
The conductor--discriminant formula and Riemann--Hurwitz therefore give
\[
 2g_n-2=-2p^n+\sum_{r=1}^n(p-1)p^{r-1}(s_r+1).
\]
Since $\sum_{r=1}^n(p-1)p^{r-1}=p^n-1$, this is
\eqref{eq:intro-genus-formula}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The break and genus formulas give
\[
 s_n\geq p^{n-1}\deg f_0,\qquad
 g_n\geq\frac{\deg f_0}{2(p+1)}(p^{2n}-1)-\frac{p^n-1}{2}.
\]
Thus the break sequence grows at least linearly in $p^n$, while the
genus sequence grows at least quadratically in $p^n$.
In the genus-stable case this also gives
$c_2\geq\deg f_0/(2(p+1))>0$.
On the other hand, both sequences can grow arbitrarily rapidly as
functions of $n$. Indeed, choose successively $f_i(X)=X^{d_i}$ with
$p\nmid d_i$ and $d_i$ as large as needed. Since $s_n\geq d_{n-1}$
and $2g_n\geq(p-1)p^{n-1}(s_n-1)$, both sequences can be made to
dominate any prescribed positive sequence. Genus stability therefore
imposes a substantial restriction.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:KW-genus}
For our $\mathbf Z_p$-tower, with reduced defining Witt vector $f$, genus stability and ramification
stability are equivalent.  More explicitly,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corrected-genus-criterion}
 \begin{split}
 \text{genus stability}
 &\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 s_n=\lambda p^{n-1}+\mu\quad(n\gg0)\\
 &\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \max_{0\leq i<n}p^{n-1-i}\deg f_i
      =\lambda p^{n-1}+\mu\quad(n\gg0),
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
for fixed rational $\lambda>0$ and $\mu\leq0$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Taking successive differences in \eqref{eq:intro-genus-formula} yields
\[
 2(g_n-g_{n-1})=(p-1)p^{n-1}(s_n-1).
\]
If $g_n=c_2p^{2n}+c_1p^n+c_0$ for all large $n$, it follows that
\[
 s_n=2c_2(p+1)p^{n-1}+2c_1+1.
\]
Conversely, substituting an eventual expression
$s_n=\lambda p^{n-1}+\mu$ into the genus formula and summing the
two geometric progressions gives an eventual polynomial of the
required form.  The finitely many earlier levels change only its
constant term.
The ramification inequality $s_{n+1}\geq ps_n$ forces
$\mu\leq0$, and $\lambda>0$ because $s_1>0$.
This proves \eqref{eq:corrected-genus-criterion} for our towers,
ramified only at infinity, without identifying genus stability with
attainment of a maximal normalized degree.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The theorem uses the genus stability criterion of Kosters--Wan
\cite{KostersWan2018} with its corrigendum
\cite{KostersWanCorrigendum}.  In particular the constant term $\mu$
in the eventual Swan conductor is allowed to be negative; requiring
$\mu=0$ would impose the stronger eventual minimal break condition.
The proof above derives the criterion for our towers directly from the genus formula.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:minimal-break}
\label{def:eventual-minimal-break}
The tower has \emph{minimal break ratios} if
\[
 s_{n+1}=ps_n
\]
for every $n\geq1$. It has \emph{eventual minimal break ratios} if
the same equality holds for every sufficiently large $n$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:attained-degree}
Our tower, with reduced defining Witt vector $f$, has eventual minimal
break ratios if and only if the normalized degrees $\deg f_i/p^i$
have a maximum. In that case, the maximum is attained at a unique
level $m$, and we write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-delta}
 \delta:=\max_{i\geq0}\frac{\deg f_i}{p^i}
        =\frac{\deg f_m}{p^m}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
If the maximum $\delta$ is attained at level $m$, then
\eqref{eq:intro-break-formula} gives
$s_n=\delta p^{n-1}$ for every $n>m$.
Conversely, if $s_{n+1}=ps_n$ for all $n\geq n_0$, then
$s_n/p^{n-1}=s_{n_0}/p^{n_0-1}$ for all $n\geq n_0$.
At level $n_0$ the finite maximum in
\eqref{eq:intro-break-formula} is attained; no later normalized
degree can exceed it.  Thus it is the global attained maximum.
For uniqueness, suppose two nonzero level polynomials $f_i,f_j$,
with $i<j$, had the same normalized degree. Then
\[
 \deg f_j=p^{j-i}\deg f_i,
\]
so $p$ would divide $\deg f_j$, contrary to the reduced condition.
Thus the maximizing level is unique.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Unless explicitly stated otherwise, from now on we assume that
our tower has eventual minimal break ratios.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:ramification-parameters}
Retain $m$ and $\delta$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:attained-degree},
and put
\[
 d=\deg f_m,\qquad \delta=\frac d{p^m}.
\]
Since $f$ is reduced, $p\nmid d$.  For $n>m$, define the stable break
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-D}
 D_n=\delta p^{n-1}=d p^{n-m-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:minimal-genus}
For $n>m$, one has $s_n=D_n$, so the local Artin conductor exponent
is $D_n+1$.  Minimal break ratios from the first level are equivalent
to $m=0$.  Eventual minimal break ratios imply genus stability,
but genus stability does not imply eventual minimal break ratios.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The break formula gives $s_n=D_n$ for $n>m$.
If $m=0$ it gives minimal ratios from the first level; conversely,
minimal ratios from the first level force the global maximum to
occur at level zero.  Theorem~\ref{thm:KW-genus}, with $\mu=0$,
gives genus stability under eventual minimal ratios.
For the example $f=\sum_{i\geq0}p^i[X]^{2p^i-1}$, the largest
term in the break formula occurs at $i=n-1$, so
$s_n=2p^{n-1}-1$ and
\[
 g_n=\frac{p^{2n}-1}{p+1}-p^n+1.
\]
This gives an explicit genus-stable tower without eventual
minimal break ratios.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:primitive-L}
Let $n\geq1$, and let $\chi_n:\mathbf Z_p\to\mathbf C_p^\times$ have exact order $p^n$. Its primitive
$L$-function is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-primitive-L}
 L_f(\chi_n,s)=
 \prod_{x\in|\mathbf A^1_{\mathbf F_q}|}
 \left(1-\chi_n(\operatorname{Frob}_x)s^{\deg x}\right)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:primitive-basics}
Let $n\geq1$, and let $\chi_n$ have exact order $p^n$.
The primitive $L$-function is a polynomial of degree $s_n-1$.
Its slopes lie in $(0,1)$ and depend only on $n$, not on the chosen
character of order $p^n$. Its slope multiset is invariant under
reflection about $1/2$. Under eventual minimal break ratios, its degree
is $D_n-1$ for $n>m$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The conductor formula for a nontrivial rank-one character on
$\mathbf A^1$, ramified only at infinity, gives a polynomial $L$-function
of degree $(s_n+1)-2=s_n-1$.
Reducing its Euler product modulo $\pi_{\chi_n}$ makes the character
trivial.  Thus the polynomial reduces to
$1/(1-qs)=1$ in the residue field.  All its nonconstant coefficients
have positive valuation, so every Newton slope is positive.
The functional equation identifies its slopes with one minus
those for $\chi_n^{-1}$.
Characters of the same order are conjugate under a cyclotomic
Galois automorphism, which preserves $p$-adic valuations.
Consequently their slope multisets agree, are invariant under reflection
about $1/2$, and contain only slopes less than one.  Finally $s_n=D_n$ for $n>m$ gives the count.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:primitive-slopes}
Normalize $v_q(q)=1$.  Write
\[
 L_f(\chi_n,s)=\prod_{j=1}^{s_n-1}(1-\beta_js).
\]
The primitive slope multiset at level $n$ is
\[
 S_n=\{v_q(\beta_1),\ldots,v_q(\beta_{s_n-1})\},
\]
with one occurrence for each reciprocal root, counted with multiplicity.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive-basics}, $S_n$ depends only on $n$, lies in
$(0,1)$, and satisfies $S_n=1-S_n$. For $n>m$ it has $D_n-1$ elements.
For a multiset $S$, the notation $cS$ scales its elements and
$S\cap I$ retains its elements in $I$ with their multiplicities.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:zeta-primitive}
For every $n\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-primitive}
 \begin{split}
 P(C_n,s)&=\prod_{r=1}^n\ \prod_{\operatorname{ord}(\chi)=p^r}
                         L_f(\chi,s),\\
 \frac{P(C_n,s)}{P(C_{n-1},s)}
          &=\prod_{\operatorname{ord}(\chi)=p^n}L_f(\chi,s).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Thus $Z(C_n,s)$ is the first product divided by $(1-s)(1-qs)$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Over $\mathbf A^1$, the regular representation of $\mathbf Z_p/p^n\mathbf Z_p$
is the direct sum of its characters.  Factoring its local Euler
factors gives the product of the corresponding $L$-functions.
The trivial character contributes $(1-qs)^{-1}$; the unique point
at infinity contributes $(1-s)^{-1}$.  Every nontrivial character
has some exact order $p^r$, giving the first identity.
Division by the same identity at level $n-1$ gives the second.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:block-formulation}
Slope stability is equivalent to the following identity for every
sufficiently large $n$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adjacent-block-stability}
 S_{n+1}=
 \bigsqcup_{j=0}^{p-1}\frac{j+S_n}{p}
 \ \sqcup\ \left\{\frac1p,\frac2p,\ldots,\frac{p-1}{p}\right\}.
\end{equation}
All unions are multiset unions.  The $j$-th propagated block is
$(j+S_n)/p\subset(j/p,(j+1)/p)$; each displayed grid slope occurs once.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Adjoin one zero to each primitive multiset.  Equation
\eqref{eq:adjacent-block-stability} then says
\[
 \{0\}\sqcup S_{n+1}
 =\bigsqcup_{j=0}^{p-1}\frac{j+(\{0\}\sqcup S_n)}p.
\]
Iteration gives Definition~\ref{def:slope-stability}, and comparing
two adjacent levels in that definition gives this identity.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:stability-necessary}
For a $\mathbf Z_p$-tower of $\mathbf P^1$ ramified only at infinity,
with reduced defining Witt vector $f$, slope stability
in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:slope-stability} implies eventual
minimal break ratios, and therefore ramification stability and genus stability.
This necessity assertion does not concern the broader progression convention
of Remark~\ref{rem:progression-multiplicities} over a different base curve.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Taking cardinalities in \eqref{eq:intro-strong-stability} gives
\[
 1+|S_n|=p^{n-n_0}(1+|S_{n_0}|).
\]
Since $|S_n|=s_n-1$, this is
$s_n=p^{n-n_0}s_{n_0}$ for all $n\geq n_0$.
Thus $s_{n+1}=ps_n$ eventually, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:KW-genus} gives genus stability.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:classical-polygon}
The normalized Newton polygon at level $n$ is
\[
 N_n=\operatorname{NP}_{\pi_{\chi_n}}C_f^*(\chi_n,s).
\]
It is the lower convex polygon determined by the coefficient points
\[
 \bigl(k,v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(b_k(\pi_{\chi_n}))\bigr),\qquad k\geq0,
\]
where $b_0(T)=1$ and the valuation of zero is $+\infty$.
More generally, $\operatorname{NP}_v$ denotes the Newton polygon of a scalar series
formed using the valuation $v$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:KZ-equivalence}
The multiset of $q$-slopes of $C_f^*(\chi_n,s)$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:characteristic-slope-union}
 \bigsqcup_{j\geq0}
 \left(\{j\}\sqcup\{j+\alpha:\alpha\in S_n\}\right).
\end{equation}
The slopes of $N_n$ are obtained by multiplying this multiset by
$a(p-1)p^{n-1}$. For $n>m$, its first $D_n$ slopes are exactly those
strictly less than $a(p-1)p^{n-1}$: they are zero followed by
$a(p-1)p^{n-1}S_n$. Its next slope is $a(p-1)p^{n-1}$, so $D_n$
is a strict vertex abscissa. Each later block is obtained by adding
$a(p-1)p^{n-1}$ to the preceding block.

The tower is slope stable if and only if the entire polygons $N_n$
are independent of $n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The factor $(1-s)L_f(\chi_n,s)$ has slopes $\{0\}\sqcup S_n$.
Replacing $s$ by $q^js$ adds $j$ to each $q$-slope; hence the product
\eqref{eq:general-C} gives \eqref{eq:characteristic-slope-union}.
All primitive slopes lie strictly between zero and one, and for $n>m$
there are $D_n-1$ of them. This proves the cutoff, vertex, and block
assertions. The equivalence with the progression identity
\eqref{eq:intro-strong-stability} is the block criterion of
\cite[Lemma 8.1]{KostersZhu2018}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:old-block}
For $n>m$, the first characteristic block at level $n$ is the
restriction of $N_n$ to $[0,D_n]$.  Its slopes are the initial zero
and the $D_n-1$ primitive slopes, multiplied by $a(p-1)p^{n-1}$.
More generally, the block indexed by $j\geq0$ occupies
$[jD_n,(j+1)D_n]$;
thus the first $b$ blocks occupy $[0,bD_n]$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:universal-reduction}
The Euler product $L_f(T,s)$ belongs to $1+s\mathbf Z_p[[T]][[s]]$.
The universal characteristic series satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:universal-C}
 \begin{split}
 C_f^*(T,s)&=\prod_{t\geq0}L_f^*(T,q^ts)
             =\sum_{k\geq0}b_k(T)s^k,\\
 C_f^*(T,s)&=L_f^*(T,s)C_f^*(T,qs).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The product is interpreted coefficientwise in the $p$-adic
topology.  It belongs to $1+s\mathbf Z_p[[T]][[s]]$, specializes to
\eqref{eq:general-C}, and has reduction
\begin{equation}\label{eq:limit-Lstar}
 \overline{C_f^*(T,s)}
 =\overline{L_f^*(T,s)}
 =(1-s)\overline{L_f(T,s)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Each Euler factor is integral, and only finitely many closed points
contribute to a fixed power of $s$, proving integrality of $L_f$.
For each fixed coefficient, the factors with large $t$ in
\eqref{eq:universal-C} approach one $p$-adically.  This proves
convergence and integrality of the product.  Removing its first
factor gives the second identity; specialization recovers the
usual characteristic series, as in \cite{LiuWan2009,KostersZhu2018}.
Reducing that identity modulo $p$ gives \eqref{eq:limit-Lstar},
since $q=0$ in the residue field and $C_f^*(T,0)=1$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:gauss-valuation}
For $u>0$ and $b(T)=\sum_jc_jT^j\in\mathbf Z_q[[T]]$, set
\[
 w_u(b(T))=\min_j\{v_p(c_j)+ju\},\qquad w_u(0)=+\infty.
\]
Here $\mathbf Z_q$ is the ring of integers in the unramified extension
of $\mathbf Q_p$ with residue field $\mathbf F_q$, and $v_p(p)=1$.
This is the Gauss valuation on the closed disc $|T|_p\leq p^{-u}$.
In particular $v_p(b(T_0))\geq w_u(b(T))$ whenever $v_p(T_0)\geq u$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:Artin-Hasse}
The Artin--Hasse exponential is the formal series
\begin{equation}\label{eq:AH}
 E(U)=\exp\left(\sum_{r\geq0}\frac{U^{p^r}}{p^r}\right)
 \in1+U\mathbf Q_p[[U]].
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:AH-integrality}
The coefficients of $E(U)$ belong to $\mathbf Z_p$, and
\[
 E(U)-1=U+O(U^2).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $\mu$ denote the M\"obius function.  Taking formal logarithms
over $\mathbf Q_p$ verifies the identity
\[
 E(U)=\prod_{\substack{r\geq1\\p\nmid r}}
          (1-U^r)^{-\mu(r)/r}.
\]
Indeed the coefficient of $U^k$ in the logarithm of the product is
$k^{-1}\sum_{r\mid k,\ p\nmid r}\mu(r)$, which is $1/k$ if $k$ is a
power of $p$ and zero otherwise.  Each exponent $-\mu(r)/r$ lies
in $\mathbf Z_p$, so the binomial coefficients in every factor are
$p$-integral.  The product converges formally, proving integrality.
The constant and linear coefficients follow from \eqref{eq:AH}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Kramer--Miller \cite{KramerMiller2026} proved that, for every prime $p$,
the reduction $\overline E(U)\in\mathbf F_p[[U]]$ is transcendental over
$\mathbf F_p(U)$, answering a question of Thakur. This gives further context
for the reduced Artin--Hasse series whose coefficients enter the
limiting Dwork operator and the explicit counterexamples below.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:AH-parameters}
For $j\geq0$, define $\pi_j(T)\in T\mathbf Z_p[[T]]$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-j}
 E(\pi_j(T))=(1+T)^{p^j}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:pi-congruence}
For every $j\geq0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-congruence}
 \pi_j(T)\equiv\pi_0(T)^{p^j}\pmod p.
\end{equation}
Since both series have zero constant term, this is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-error}
 \pi_j(T)-\pi_0(T)^{p^j}\in pT\mathbf Z_p[[T]].
\end{equation}
Thus the reduction of $\pi_j(T)$ has $T$-adic order $p^j$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Reducing \eqref{eq:pi-inverse-relation} modulo $p$ gives
\[
 \pi_j(T)\equiv\pi_0(T^{p^j})
             \equiv\pi_0(T)^{p^j}\pmod p.
\]
Both series have zero constant term, so their difference belongs to
$pT\mathbf Z_p[[T]]$. Since $\pi_0(T)=T+O(T^2)$, the reduced order is $p^j$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:pi-specialization}
Let $\chi_n:\mathbf Z_p\to\mathbf C_p^\times$ have exact order $p^n$, where $n\geq1$,
and put
\[
 \pi_{\chi_n}=\chi_n(1)-1,
 \qquad v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(\pi_{\chi_n})=1.
\]
Then the series $\pi_j(T)$ converge at $T=\pi_{\chi_n}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-specialization}
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}\bigl(\pi_j(\pi_{\chi_n})\bigr)=p^j
 \quad(0\leq j<n),
 \qquad
 \pi_j(\pi_{\chi_n})=0\quad(j\geq n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The integral series $\pi_j(T)$ converge at $\pi_{\chi_n}$.
Writing $\chi_n(1)=\zeta_{p^n}$, the inverse relation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-character-meaning}
 \pi_j(\pi_{\chi_n})=\pi_0(\zeta_{p^n}^{\,p^j}-1).
\end{equation}
An integral change of variable $U+O(U^2)$ preserves every positive
valuation. For $j<n$, the root of unity on the right has order
$p^{n-j}$, hence
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}\bigl(\pi_j(\pi_{\chi_n})\bigr)
 =\frac{v_p(\zeta_{p^{n-j}}-1)}{v_p(\zeta_{p^n}-1)}=p^j.
\]
For $j\geq n$ its argument is zero, so the parameter vanishes.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:parameter-zeros}
In the open unit disc $|T_0|_p<1$, the zeros of $\pi_j(T_0)$ are
exactly
\[
 T_0=\zeta-1,\qquad \zeta^{p^j}=1.
\]
All $p^j$ zeros are simple; for $j=0$ the only zero is $T_0=0$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The quotient in \eqref{eq:pi-leading-unit} is an integral power series
with constant term one, so it is a unit at every point of the open
unit disc. Thus $\pi_j(T_0)$ vanishes precisely when
$(1+T_0)^{p^j}-1=0$. Differentiating
\eqref{eq:pi-inverse-relation} at $T_0=\zeta-1$ gives
$\pi_j'(\zeta-1)=p^j\zeta^{-1}\ne0$, proving simplicity.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:gauss-parameters}
For every $i\geq0$ and $u>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-parameters}
 w_u\bigl(\pi_i(T)\bigr)=\min_{0\leq r\leq i}\{r+p^{i-r}u\}.
\end{equation}
In particular $w_u(\pi_i(T))\longrightarrow\infty$ as
$i\longrightarrow\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:pi-leading-unit},
\[
 w_u\bigl(\pi_i(T)\bigr)
 =w_u\bigl((1+T)^{p^i}-1\bigr)
 =\min_{1\leq k\leq p^i}
       \left\{v_p\binom{p^i}{k}+ku\right\}.
\]
For $1\leq k\leq p^i$ one has
\[
 \binom{p^i}{k}=\frac{p^i}{k}\binom{p^i-1}{k-1},
 \qquad v_p\binom{p^i}{k}=i-v_p(k).
\]
The second binomial coefficient is a unit: modulo $p$,
$(1+T)^{p^i-1}=\sum_{j=0}^{p^i-1}(-T)^j$, so none of its
coefficients vanishes. Among the indices with $v_p(k)=s$, the
smallest is $k=p^s$, and this index minimizes $ku$. Thus the
Gauss valuation is
\[
 \min_{0\leq s\leq i}\{i-s+p^su\}
 =\min_{0\leq r\leq i}\{r+p^{i-r}u\},
\]
as claimed. To prove divergence, fix a real bound $B\geq0$.
Terms with $r>B$ already exceed $B$. For the finitely many integers
$0\leq r\leq B$, the quantities $p^{i-r}u$ tend to infinity with
$i$. Hence the displayed minimum tends to infinity.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{def:splitting-function}
For the reduced defining Witt vector $f$, its splitting function is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:universal-splitting}
 F(T,X)=\prod_{i,\ell}E\bigl(\pi_i(T)[a_{i,\ell}]X^\ell\bigr)
       =\sum_{\nu\geq0}\eta_\nu(T)X^\nu,
 \qquad \eta_\nu(T)=0\quad(\nu<0).
\end{equation}
Here $\eta_\nu(T)\in\mathbf Z_q[[T]]$ is the coefficient of $X^\nu$.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:splitting-identity}
For $t\in\mathbf F_{q^r}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:universal-splitting-character}
 \prod_{h=0}^{ar-1}F^{\sigma^h}(T,[t]^{p^h})
 =(1+T)^{\operatorname{Tr}_{W(\mathbf F_{q^r})/\mathbf Z_p}f(t)}.
\end{equation}
Superscripts $\sigma^h$ act on coefficients.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Consider one monomial at Witt level $i$. For every $j\geq0$,
\[
 \sum_{h=0}^{ar-1}([a_{i,\ell}][t]^\ell)^{p^{h+j}}
 =\operatorname{Tr}_{W(\mathbf F_{q^r})/\mathbf Z_p}
      ([a_{i,\ell}][t]^\ell).
\]
Taking formal logarithms of its Artin--Hasse factors and using
\eqref{eq:AH} gives this trace times
$\log E(\pi_i(T))=p^i\log(1+T)$. Exponentiating proves the monomial
identity, and multiplication over the monomials proves
\eqref{eq:universal-splitting-character}. The infinite-level identity
follows by the convergence just established.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:splitting-matrix-bound}
Let $w$ be one of the Gauss, classical, unreduced $T$-adic, or reduced
$T$-adic valuations used here. The Artin--Hasse coefficients and
Teichm\"uller coefficients (or their reductions) are integral for these
valuations. Let $g$ be a nonnegative function on $\mathbf R_{\geq0}$
with $g(0)=0$, and suppose it is subadditive, meaning
\[
 g(x+y)\leq g(x)+g(y)\qquad(x,y\geq0).
\]
For a finite splitting product, suppose
$w(\pi_i(T))\geq g(\ell)$ for every monomial of degree $\ell$ at level $i$.
Then
\[
 w(\eta_\nu(T))\geq g(\nu),\qquad
 w(\eta_{pi-j}(T))\geq g(pi)-g(j)\quad(i,j\geq0).
\]
The same assertions hold after specialization, with
$\pi_i(T_0)$ and $\eta_\nu(T_0)$, or after reduction modulo $p$, with
$\overline{\pi_i(T)}$ and $\overline{\eta_\nu(T)}$, whenever the stated
parameter bounds hold. They also pass to any convergent coefficient limit.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Write $E(U)=\sum_{r\geq0}e_rU^r$. A contribution of degree $r\ell$
from one factor is $e_r[a_{i,\ell}]^r\pi_i(T)^r$, of valuation at least
$r g(\ell)\geq g(r\ell)$. In a product of contributions, repeated
subadditivity bounds the sum of their weights below by $g$ of the total
degree. Every contribution to $\eta_\nu(T)$ therefore has valuation at
least $g(\nu)$, and so does their sum. If $pi-j\geq0$, subadditivity gives
$g(pi)\leq g(pi-j)+g(j)$, proving the entry bound. If $pi-j<0$, the
entry is zero and the bound still holds. This argument applies to each
of the stated coefficient rings and is preserved under convergent limits.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:finite-dwork-convergence}
For each $u>0$, the operator $\Psi(T)^a$ of a finite Witt truncation
is completely continuous on a suitable weighted Banach space over the
completed Gauss-valued coefficient field. Its traces and Fredholm
expansions converge.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Fix $u>0$. Because the splitting product is finite and every active parameter
has positive Gauss valuation, choose a positive integer $e$ so large
that $b=1/e$ is strictly smaller than every ratio
$w_u(\pi_i(T))/\ell$ occurring in it. We may extend the coefficient
field by a root $p^{1/e}$, extend Frobenius by fixing this root, and
use the Gauss valuation on that extension.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:splitting-matrix-bound} with $g(x)=bx$ to obtain
$w_u(\eta_\nu(T))\geq b\nu$.
Extend the multiplicative Gauss valuation $w_u$ to the fraction
field of $\mathbf Z_q[[T]][p^{1/e}]$, and complete this valued field.
Coefficient Frobenius extends continuously and isometrically to
the resulting complete nonarchimedean field.  Over this field use
the weighted Banach space
\[
 \left\{\sum_{j\geq0}c_j(T)X^j:
       w_u(c_j(T))-bj\longrightarrow+\infty\right\},
 \qquad
 \left\|\sum_jc_j(T)X^j\right\|_b
       =\sup_j p^{-w_u(c_j(T))+bj}.
\]
The vectors $p^{j/e}X^j$ form an orthonormal basis for this space:
the coordinates $p^{-j/e}c_j(T)$ tend to zero. Thus the usual
Fredholm construction on the space of null sequences applies.
The scalar extension does not change the principal-minor coefficients;
the introduced basis factors cancel in every principal determinant.
Here ``Banach space'' means a space over the complete valued field,
rather than a module over the uncompleted integral coefficient ring. The contribution of the $(i,j)$-entry to the operator
norm is measured by
\[
 \frac{\|\eta_{pi-j}(T)X^i\|_b}{\|X^j\|_b}
 =p^{-w_u(\eta_{pi-j}(T))+b(i-j)}.
\]
The scalar valuation is still $w_u$; the extra term comes from the
weights of the input and output basis vectors. Its negative logarithm
satisfies
\[
 w_u(\eta_{pi-j}(T))+b(j-i)\geq b(p-1)i
 \qquad(j\leq pi),
\]
and entries with $j>pi$ vanish. Thus the weighted row norms of $M(T)$,
computed with respect to the displayed Banach norm, satisfy
\[
 \sup_{j\geq0}p^{-w_u(\eta_{pi-j}(T))+b(i-j)}
 \leq p^{-b(p-1)i}\longrightarrow0.
\]
These are the row norms after the basis normalization; the ordinary
rows of $M(T)$ contain $\eta_0(T)=1$ and do not tend to zero.
Coefficient Frobenius preserves the estimate, so it applies to
$M(T)^{\sigma^{-1}}$ as well. Truncating to finitely many rows
therefore approximates the operator in norm.  The linear operator $\Psi(T)^a$ is therefore completely
continuous, and its Fredholm expansions converge.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:dwork-trace}
For a finite Witt truncation, the operator above satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dwork-trace}
 (q^r-1)\operatorname{Tr}((\Psi(T)^a)^r)
 =\sum_{t\in\mathbf F_{q^r}^{\times}}
 (1+T)^{\operatorname{Tr}_{W(\mathbf F_{q^r})/\mathbf Z_p}f(t)}
 \qquad(r\geq1).
\end{equation}

Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-Fredholm}
 C_f^*(T,s)=\det(1-s\Psi(T)^a)=\det(1-sM_q(T)).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
To see the trace identity explicitly, expand the finite splitting product
\[
 \prod_{h=0}^{ar-1}F^{\sigma^h}(T,X^{p^h})
   =\sum_{\nu\geq0}c_\nu(T)X^\nu.
\]
The nonzero Teichm\"uller lifts are the $(q^r-1)$-st roots of unity, so
\[
 \sum_{t\in\mathbf F_{q^r}^{\times}}[t]^\nu
 =\begin{cases}q^r-1,&(q^r-1)\mid\nu,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:universal-splitting-character}, this makes the
right side of \eqref{eq:dwork-trace} equal to
$(q^r-1)\sum_{j\geq0}c_{(q^r-1)j}(T)$.
On the operator side, use the coefficient-selection identity
\[
 \psi_p\bigl(g(T,X^p)h(T,X)\bigr)
 =g(T,X)\psi_p\bigl(h(T,X)\bigr)
\]
and $\sigma^{ar}=1$ to obtain
\[
 \Psi(T)^{ar}(X^j)
 =\psi_p^{ar}\left(\sum_{\nu\geq0}c_\nu(T)X^{\nu+j}\right)
 =\sum_{i\geq0}c_{q^ri-j}(T)X^i.
\]
Here negative subscripts mean zero. The $j$-th diagonal entry is
$c_{(q^r-1)j}(T)$; summing the diagonal proves
\eqref{eq:dwork-trace}. The convergence of these sums follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-dwork-convergence}.
The sum excludes zero, in accordance with the starred $L$-function.
The logarithmic determinant identity is
\[
 \log\det(1-s\Psi(T)^a)
 =-\sum_{r\geq1}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((\Psi(T)^a)^r\bigr)\frac{s^r}{r}.
\]
Substituting \eqref{eq:dwork-trace} identifies this with the logarithm
of \eqref{eq:universal-C}, proving \eqref{eq:general-Fredholm}.

See \cite[Theorem 5.5 and Corollary 5.6]{KostersZhu2018}.
For $q=p$, the coefficient twist is trivial and this becomes
$C_f^*(T,s)=\det(1-sM(T))$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:cyclic-minor-bound}
In a convergent Fredholm expansion as above, suppose that coefficient
Frobenius preserves a valuation $w$, meaning
\[
 w\bigl(c(T)^\sigma\bigr)=w(c(T))
\]
for every coefficient series in the valued ring under consideration,
and suppose that $w(\eta_{pi-j}(T))\geq g(pi)-g(j)$.
Here $\sigma$ acts on coefficients and fixes $T$. For $w_u$ the equality
follows from $v_p(\sigma(c_j))=v_p(c_j)$ in every coefficient. Every closed product indexed by
$I_0,\ldots,I_a=I_0$ has valuation at least
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{a-1}\sum_{i\in I_r}\bigl(g(pi)-g(i)\bigr).
\]
If $g(pi)-g(i)$ is nondecreasing for integers $i\geq0$, then
\[
 w(b_k(T))\geq a\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\bigl(g(pi)-g(i)\bigr).
\]
The same conclusion holds for specialized or reduced coefficients when
the corresponding expansion and entry estimates hold.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
In each determinant term with rows $I_r$ and columns $I_{r+1}$, every
row and column occurs once. Its valuation is consequently at least
\[
 \sum_{i\in I_r}g(pi)-\sum_{j\in I_{r+1}}g(j).
\]
The valuation inequality gives the same bound for the minor. Adding over
the $a$ minors cancels the column sums against the next row sums because
$I_a=I_0$, leaving the first displayed bound. The $k$ elements of each
$I_r$, listed in increasing order, are at least $0,1,\ldots,k-1$.
Monotonicity therefore gives the second bound for every closed product
and hence for their convergent sum. The auxiliary basis weights cancel
as above and do not alter this calculation.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:classical-reduced-coefficients}
Assume $\deg f_i\leq\delta p^i$. At a character of order $p^n$,
\[
 \begin{split}
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(\eta_\nu(\pi_{\chi_n}))&\geq\nu/\delta,\\
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(\eta_{pi-j}(\pi_{\chi_n}))
 &\geq(pi-j)/\delta,\\
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(b_k(\pi_{\chi_n}))
 &\geq\frac{a(p-1)}{2\delta}k(k-1).
 \end{split}
\]
After reduction modulo $p$, the same bounds hold with
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{\eta_\nu(T)}$,
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{\eta_{pi-j}(T)}$, and
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}$, respectively.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
For the classical specialization, only levels $i<n$ remain, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:pi-specialization} gives parameter valuation $p^i$.
For the reduction, Lemma~\ref{lem:pi-congruence} gives parameter order
$p^i$. In both cases $p^i\geq\ell/\delta$, so apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:splitting-matrix-bound} with $g(x)=x/\delta$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-minor-bound} then gives the coefficient bound,
since $g(pi)-g(i)=(p-1)i/\delta$.

For completeness, the reduced infinite product converges coefficientwise:
its level-$i$ factors differ from one in $T$-adic order at least $p^i$.
The same linear degree estimate, with any smaller positive basis weight,
makes its weighted row norms tend to zero, just as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-dwork-convergence}. Its Fredholm coefficients thus
converge. They agree with $\overline{b_k(T)}$: reduce the finite-truncation
identities and pass to the $T$-adic limit. On the Euler-product side this
limit follows directly from
$(1+T)^{p^N z}\equiv(1+T^{p^N})^z\pmod p$ for $z\in\mathbf Z_p$.
Thus the bound applies to the full reduced series as well.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:truncation-convergence}
For every $u>0$, each coefficient of $L_f(T,s)$ and $C_f^*(T,s)$ is the
$w_u$-limit of the corresponding coefficients for finite Witt truncations.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
At any fixed closed point of $\mathbf A^1$, truncating after level
$N-1$ changes the Frobenius exponent by an element of $p^N\mathbf Z_p$.
For $z\in\mathbf Z_p$, the series
\[
 (1+T)^{p^Nz}-1
 =\sum_{r\geq1}\binom zr\bigl((1+T)^{p^N}-1\bigr)^r
\]
has Gauss valuation at least that of $(1+T)^{p^N}-1$, which tends
to infinity by the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:gauss-parameters}.
Thus the truncated character values converge in $w_u$, uniformly
in the omitted exponent $z$.

Only finitely many Euler factors contribute to any fixed coefficient
of $L_f(T,s)$, so its truncated coefficients converge in $w_u$.
In the product \eqref{eq:universal-C}, the nonconstant coefficient
of degree $j\geq1$ in a factor with argument $q^ts$ has Gauss
valuation at least $atj$: replacing $s$ by $q^ts$ multiplies its
degree-$j$ coefficient by
\[
 (q^t)^j=q^{tj}=p^{atj},
\]
while the original coefficient is integral. Thus the factors with large $t$ tend
uniformly to one coefficient by coefficient, independently of
the Witt truncation.  It follows that each $b_k(T)$ is the
Gauss-norm limit of its truncated counterparts.  This coefficientwise limiting process will allow the bounds proved for
finite truncations to pass to the full defining equation.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:concave-weight}
For $x\geq0$ put
\[
 g_u(x)=\min_{r\geq0}\left\{r+\frac{ux}{\delta p^r}\right\}.
\]
This function is increasing and concave downward, has $g_u(0)=0$,
and is subadditive, meaning
\[
 g_u(x+y)\leq g_u(x)+g_u(y)\qquad(x,y\geq0).
\]
If $\ell\leq\delta p^i$, then
\[
 w_u(\pi_i(T))\geq g_u(\ell).
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:concave-increment}
 g_u(px)-g_u(x)=\min\{\frac{(p-1)ux}{\delta},1\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The minimum is attained because the expressions tend to infinity
with $r$.  Each is increasing and affine in $x$, so their minimum
is increasing and concave downward.  Explicitly, for $x,y\geq0$
and $0\leq\theta\leq1$, each affine expression at
$\theta x+(1-\theta)y$ is at least
$\theta g_u(x)+(1-\theta)g_u(y)$.  Taking the minimum gives
\[
 g_u(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)
 \geq\theta g_u(x)+(1-\theta)g_u(y).
\]
Thus the graph lies above its chords.  The relevant fact is that
each affine function is concave and pointwise minima preserve
concavity; convexity alone would not suffice.

Concavity and $g_u(0)=0$ imply
\[
 g_u(x)\geq\frac{x}{x+y}g_u(x+y),\qquad
 g_u(y)\geq\frac{y}{x+y}g_u(x+y)
\]
when $x+y>0$.  Adding gives
$g_u(x+y)\leq g_u(x)+g_u(y)$; the case $x=y=0$ is immediate.
For the parameter assertion, $\ell\leq\delta p^i$ gives
$p^{i-r}u\geq u\ell/(\delta p^r)$ for $0\leq r\leq i$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:gauss-parameters}, then enlarge the set over
which the minimum is taken from $0\leq r\leq i$ to all $r\geq0$.
This proves $w_u(\pi_i(T))\geq g_u(\ell)$.

It remains to compute the increment.  Separating $r=0$ and
reindexing the remaining terms gives
\[
 g_u(px)=\min\{pux/\delta,\ 1+g_u(x)\}.
\]
If $(p-1)ux/\delta\leq1$, then for every integer $r\geq1$,
\[
 \frac{ux}{\delta}(1-p^{-r})\leq1\leq r,
 \qquad
 r+\frac{ux}{\delta p^r}\geq\frac{ux}{\delta}.
\]
The minimum defining $g_u(x)$ is therefore attained at $r=0$, so
$g_u(x)=ux/\delta$.  Substituting this into the formula for $g_u(px)$ gives
\[
 g_u(px)-g_u(x)
 =\min\{(p-1)ux/\delta,1\}=(p-1)ux/\delta.
\]
If $(p-1)ux/\delta\geq1$, the general bound $g_u(x)\leq ux/\delta$ gives
\[
 \frac{pux}{\delta}-g_u(x)\geq\frac{(p-1)ux}{\delta}\geq1.
\]
In this case the increment is one.  The two cases prove
\eqref{eq:concave-increment}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:uniform-gauss}
For $C_f^*(T,s)=\sum_{k\geq0}b_k(T)s^k$ and every $u>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-gauss}
 w_u(b_k(T))\geq a\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\min\{\frac{(p-1)uj}{\delta},1\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Fix $u>0$ and first retain only finitely many Witt levels.
Lemma~\ref{lem:concave-weight} gives $w_u(\pi_i(T))\geq g_u(\ell)$
for each monomial. Lemma~\ref{lem:splitting-matrix-bound} therefore gives
$w_u(\eta_\nu(T))\geq g_u(\nu)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gauss-matrix-entry}
 w_u(\eta_{pi-j}(T))\geq g_u(pi-j)\geq g_u(pi)-g_u(j)
 \qquad(pi-j\geq0).
\end{equation}
For a negative subscript the entry is zero, so the final bound still
holds. Coefficient Frobenius preserves $w_u$, and
\eqref{eq:concave-increment} shows that the increments are
\[
 g_u(pi)-g_u(i)=\min\left\{\frac{(p-1)ui}{\delta},1\right\},
\]
which increase with $i$. The convergent determinant of
Theorem~\ref{thm:dwork-trace} and Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-minor-bound}
now prove \eqref{eq:uniform-gauss} for the finite truncation.

Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:truncation-convergence} identifies $b_k(T)$
with the Gauss-norm limit of its truncated counterparts. The bound is
independent of the truncation, so it passes to this limit. This passage
uses convergence of coefficients and does not require the full infinite
Witt operator to be completely continuous at arbitrary weights.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:formal-nonmeromorphy}
Over $\mathbf F_p$, the tower
\[
 f=[X]+\sum_{\substack{\ell\geq2\\\ell\text{ prime}}}
                   p^\ell[X]^{p^\ell-1}
\]
has minimal break ratios, with $\delta=1$. Its $T$-adic $L$-function
is not meromorphic for the unreduced $T$-adic valuation, and its
characteristic series is not entire for that valuation.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
This is reduced and has attained normalized degree $\delta=1$, hence
minimal break ratios. To compute its linear coefficient in $T$, start with
\[
 [Ts^r]\log L_f(T,s)
 =\frac1r\sum_{x\in\mathbf F_{p^r}}
       \operatorname{Tr}_{W(\mathbf F_{p^r})/\mathbf Z_p} f(x).
\]
The value at zero is zero. For a positive integer $k$, the sum over
nonzero Teichm\"uller lifts is
\[
 \sum_{x\in\mathbf F_{p^r}^{\times}}[x]^k
 =\begin{cases}p^r-1,&p^r-1\mid k,\\0,&p^r-1\nmid k.\end{cases}
\]
The trace of this sum is $r$ times the sum, since it lies in $\mathbf Z_p$.
This cancels the factor $1/r$ above; the cancellation is made after
summing, not by replacing an individual trace with $r$ times its input.
For a tail exponent $p^\ell-1$, the divisibility condition is
\[
 p^r-1\mid p^\ell-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\mid\ell.
\]
Indeed, writing $\ell=ar+b$ with $0\leq b<r$, reduction modulo
$p^r-1$ leaves $p^b-1$, which is zero only when $b=0$.
If $r\geq2$ and $\ell$ is prime, this forces $r=\ell$.
The initial monomial gives zero for $r\geq2$. Therefore
\[
 [Ts^r]\log L_f(T,s)=
 \begin{cases}p^r(p^r-1),&r\text{ prime},\\0,&r\text{ composite},\end{cases}
 \qquad r\geq2.
\]
The infinite sum is legitimate because its Witt coefficients tend to
zero $p$-adically; for each $r\geq2$ the displayed calculation leaves
at most one nonzero tail contribution.

The series $[T]\log L_f(T,s)$ is not rational in $s$. Indeed, the
coefficients of a rational power series satisfy a fixed linear
recurrence from some index onward. If its order is $k$,
then a block of $k$ consecutive zeros beyond that index forces every
subsequent coefficient to be zero, by induction in the recurrence.
Here there are arbitrarily long blocks of composite integers
(for example, $(k+1)!+2,\ldots,(k+1)!+k+1$), but infinitely many
prime indices with nonzero coefficient. This is a contradiction.
Only this elementary recurrence observation is needed.
Suppose instead that $L_f(T,s)=A(T,s)/B(T,s)$ with both $A$ and
$B$ entire for the unreduced $T$-adic valuation. The minimum
$T$-order of the coefficients of each is finite and attained.
Since $L_f(0,s)=(1-ps)^{-1}\ne0$, the identity $A=L_fB$ forces
these two minimum orders to be equal: reducing at the first nonzero
$T$-order multiplies the nonzero reduction of $B$ by the nonzero
series $(1-ps)^{-1}$. Multiplying both $A$ and $B$ by the same
power of $T$ therefore makes their minimum orders zero.
Write their first two terms as
\[
 A(T,s)=A_0(s)+T A_1(s)+O(T^2),\qquad
 B(T,s)=B_0(s)+T B_1(s)+O(T^2).
\]
Each $A_i(s),B_i(s)$ in this display is a polynomial: entireness
forces the $T$-orders of the $s$-coefficients to tend to infinity.
Moreover $A_0,B_0$ are nonzero. Differentiating the quotient at
$T=0$ now gives
\[
 [T]\log L_f(T,s)=\frac{A_1(s)}{A_0(s)}-
                         \frac{B_1(s)}{B_0(s)},
\]
a rational function of $s$, contrary to the recurrence argument. Finally, if $C_f^*(T,s)$ were $T$-adic entire, the
identity
$L_f(T,s)=C_f^*(T,s)/((1-s)C_f^*(T,qs))$ would give just such a
meromorphic expression. Thus it is not $T$-adic entire in this example.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{def:hodge-constants}
With the parameters in Definition~\ref{def:ramification-parameters}, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-constants}
 h(k)=\frac{a(p-1)}{2\delta}k(k-1).
\end{equation}
We use the same quadratic expression for real arguments.
The degree-gap constant $C$ in \eqref{eq:KZ-gap-constant} also bounds the vertical distance
between the Hodge and contact polygons after division by $\delta$;
the bound is $C/\delta$.
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{def:limiting-polygon}
Recall the universal characteristic series
$C_f^*(T,s)\in1+s\mathbf Z_p[[T]][[s]]$ of Section~\ref{sec:weight-space}.
A bar denotes coefficientwise reduction modulo $p$.  Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:limit-polygon}
 N_\infty=\operatorname{NP}_T\!\left(\overline{C_f^*(T,s)}\right),
\end{equation}
where $\operatorname{ord}_T(T)=1$ on $\mathbf F_p((T))$.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{def:weight-polygon}
For $T_0\in\mathbf C_p$ with $0<|T_0|_p<1$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weight-polygon}
 N(T_0)=\frac1{v_p(T_0)}\operatorname{NP}_{v_p}C_f^*(T_0,s).
\end{equation}
This is the lower convex polygon of the specialized coefficient
points, whether or not the series is entire in $s$.
At $T_0=\chi_n(1)-1$ it equals $N_n$.
By the Newton polygon theorem, its slopes $\lambda<a/v_p(T_0)$ correspond,
with multiplicity, to zeros $s_0$ in $|s|_p<q$, with
\[
 v_p(s_0^{-1})=-v_p(s_0)=v_p(T_0)\lambda.
\]
Indeed $|s_0|_p<q=p^a$ is equivalent to $v_p(T_0)\lambda<a$.
The horizontal length of a segment records the number of zeros
with that reciprocal-root valuation, counted with multiplicity.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:limit-polygon}
Assume that the tower has eventual minimal break ratios.
For every integer $K\geq1$,
\[
 N(T_0)|_{[0,K]}=N_\infty|_{[0,K]}
 \qquad\text{for all sufficiently small }v_p(T_0)>0.
\]
An explicit boundary annulus is given in
Corollary~\ref{cor:annulus-width}.
In particular $N_n|_{[0,K]}=N_\infty|_{[0,K]}$ for all sufficiently
large $n$.
For $n>m$, the classical polygons $N_n$ and $N_\infty$ have the common contact vertices
\[
 N_n(k)=N_\infty(k)=h(k)\qquad(k\equiv0,1\pmod d).
\]
At every nonnegative integer $k$, the polygons $N_n$ for $n>m$ and
$N_\infty$ lie between $h(k)$ and $h(k)+C/\delta$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{def:agreement-radius}
For a nonzero weight $T_0$ in the open unit disc, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weight-radius}
 R(T_0)=\sup\{R\geq0:N(T_0)|_{[0,R]}=N_\infty|_{[0,R]}\}
 \in[0,\infty].
\end{equation}
At a classical weight of conductor $p^n$, with $n>m$, put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:agreement-radius}
 R_n=R(\chi_n(1)-1)
 =\sup\{R\geq0:N_n|_{[0,R]}=N_\infty|_{[0,R]}\}.
\end{equation}
Thus $R_n=\infty$ precisely when $N_n=N_\infty$ on the entire half-line.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:radius-stationarity}
Under eventual minimal break ratios, $R_n\to\infty$.
Strong slope stability is equivalent to $R_n=\infty$ for every
sufficiently large $n$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{def:contact-polygons}
The Hodge polygon is the polygon joining $(k,h(k))$ for all
integers $k\geq0$.  The contact polygon joins only those points
whose abscissas satisfy $k\equiv0,1\pmod d$, in increasing order.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:general-Hodge-contact}
Assume that the tower has eventual minimal break ratios, and let $r>m$.
The polygon $N_r$ lies above the Hodge polygon and below the contact
polygon.  Every contact is a vertex of $N_r$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-contact}
 h(k)\leq N_r(k)\leq h(k)+C/\delta\quad(k\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0}),\qquad
 N_r(k)=h(k)\quad(k\equiv0,1\pmod d).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The lower bound follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:classical-reduced-coefficients}; the exact contact
vertices are \cite[Proposition 6.2]{KostersZhu2018}, with ordinates
normalized by $v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(\pi_{\chi_r})=1$ and conductor
restricted to $r>m$. This contact theorem is the common external
input to the coefficient comparisons, the unit residue blocks in
Part~\ref{part:examples}, and the semilinear blocks in
Part~\ref{part:uniform}.
Convexity bounds $N_r$ above by each chord joining consecutive
contacts.  It remains to verify the displayed uniform gap, as in
\cite[Lemma 8.2]{KostersZhu2018}.
Between $td$ and $td+1$ both comparison polygons agree.
For $k=td+u$, $1\leq u\leq d$, the chord from $td+1$ to $(t+1)d$
lies above the quadratic ordinate by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-chord-gap}
 \frac{a(p-1)}{2\delta}(u-1)(d-u)
 \leq\frac{a(p-1)(d-1)^2}{8\delta}=\frac C\delta.
\end{equation}
At integer $k$ this proves the asserted bound.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:DWX-stability}
Suppose $f_i=0$ for $i>0$ and $f_0$ is a reduced monic polynomial
of degree $d$ prime to $p$, represented by its Teichm\"uller lift.
Let $n_0$ be the least positive integer such that
\[
 p^{n_0-1}\geq\frac{a(d-1)^2}{8d}.
\]
Then $N_n=N_\infty$ on the entire half-line for every $n\geq n_0$.
Equivalently, $R_n=\infty$ for every $n\geq n_0$, and the tower is
slope stable with starting level $n_0$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:DWX-constant}
The numerical gap is the same after normalization; the hypotheses
and the resulting agreement ranges differ.
For a Teichm\"uller polynomial tower, $m=0$ and $\delta=d$.
Davis--Wan--Xiao divide our ordinates by $a(p-1)$, so
\eqref{eq:general-chord-gap} becomes
\[
 \frac{(u-1)(d-u)}{2d}\leq\frac{(d-1)^2}{8d}.
\]
Their bound in \cite[Lemma 3.7]{DavisWanXiao2016}, multiplied by
$a(p-1)$, is exactly $C/d=a(p-1)(d-1)^2/(8d)$.
The coefficient comparison in this part does not improve this
vertical gap estimate. The later semilinear argument improves the
classical constants and starting levels without changing this
geometric chord bound or the arbitrary-weight comparison below.

The polynomial conclusion is stronger.  For $d>1$, the comparison in our normalization is
\begin{center}\small
\renewcommand{1.35}{1.5}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Hypothesis on the tower & Condition on $v_p(T_0)$ & Agreement with $N_\infty$\\
\midrule
Teichm\"uller polynomial
 & $0<v_p(T_0)\leq d/C$ & Entire half-line\\
Eventual minimal breaks
 & $0<v_p(T_0)<\delta/[C+(p-1)(M-1)]$ & $[0,M]$, at a contact $M\geq2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The first row is \cite[Theorem 3.8 and Remark 3.9]{DavisWanXiao2016};
the second is Theorem~\ref{thm:annular-agreement}.
The polynomial theorem allows a larger annulus, independent of $M$,
and fixes the whole polygon there.  The general theorem applies
to infinitely many Witt levels, where full agreement can fail.
For $d=1$ or $d=2$, every nonnegative integer is a contact index.
Thus the classical polygons and the limiting polygon equal the Hodge
polygon at every level $n>m$, and $R_n=\infty$. For $d=2$ the actual
gap between the Hodge and contact polygons is zero, even though the
coarser numerical bound $C$ is positive.

The coefficient estimates explain the difference.  In the polynomial
case, the unreduced coefficient bound $\operatorname{ord}_T b_k(T)\geq h(k)$ holds for every $k\geq0$, and
$1/v_p(T_0)\geq C/\delta$ excludes interfering $p$-divisible terms uniformly.
For the general family, our estimate through $M$ instead requires
$1/v_p(T_0)-\frac{(p-1)(M-1)}{\delta}>C/\delta$.  Its additional index-dependent term is why
the guaranteed annulus shrinks with $M$.

At a classical weight the polynomial condition is
$p^{n-1}\geq a(d-1)^2/(8d)$, giving full stability.
Our general conclusion is agreement through $D_n-A$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:DWX-constant-comparison}
 A=d\left\lceil\frac{a(d-1)^2}{8d}\right\rceil.
\end{equation}
Thus $A$ is a horizontal loss obtained by rounding the same
normalized gap to the contact spacing; it is not a competing
conductor threshold.  For example, with $p=7$, $a=1$, $d=11$,
and $m=0$, one has $C/\delta=75/11$, $A=22$, and $D_2=77$.
The polynomial theorem gives $R_n=\infty$ for $n\geq2$;
our general bound gives $R_2\geq55$.
Corollary~\ref{cor:degree-eleven-loss} improves this to $R_2\geq67$
for every tower with these parameters, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-loss} shows that the improved bound is sharp.
The examples show why the full polynomial conclusion does not
extend to all towers with eventual minimal breaks.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:reduced-specialization}
Let $b(T)\in\mathbf Z_p[[T]]$ and let $\pi$ have positive $p$-adic valuation,
normalized by $v_\pi(\pi)=1$. Then
\[
 v_\pi(b(\pi))\geq
 \min\{\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b(T)},\,v_\pi(p)\},
\]
with equality whenever
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b(T)}<v_\pi(p)$.
The order of the zero series is $+\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Write $b(T)=\sum_jc_jT^j$. If the first coefficient that is a unit
modulo $p$ has index $\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b(T)}<v_\pi(p)$,
its specialized term has exactly that valuation. Earlier coefficients
are divisible by $p$ and give strictly larger valuations; later
terms have larger degree and hence also larger valuation.
This is the unique term of minimum valuation.
If $\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b(T)}\geq v_\pi(p)$, every term
of degree less than $v_\pi(p)$ has coefficient divisible by $p$,
and every remaining term already has degree at least $v_\pi(p)$.
Thus every term, and their convergent sum, has valuation at least
$v_\pi(p)$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:limit-contacts}
The polygon $N_\infty$ lies between the Hodge polygon and the
contact polygon.  At every integer $k\geq0$,
\[
 h(k)\leq N_\infty(k)\leq h(k)+C/\delta.
\]
At each $k\equiv0,1\pmod d$ it has a vertex of height $h(k)$, and
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}=h(k)$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Corollary~\ref{cor:classical-reduced-coefficients} gives
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}\geq h(k)$ for every $k$,
so the reduced polygon lies above the Hodge polygon.
At a contact index $k\equiv0,1\pmod d$, choose $n>m$ with
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(p)=(p-1)p^{n-1}>h(k).
\]
The classical coefficient has valuation exactly $h(k)$ because the
contact is a vertex. Lemma~\ref{lem:reduced-specialization} forces
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}=h(k)$: a smaller reduced order
would give that smaller specialized valuation, while a larger order
would give a specialized valuation strictly greater than $h(k)$.
Thus the polygon of the reduced series has all the same contacts
and lies between the Hodge lower polygon and the polygon joining
successive contacts.  This also proves its stated upper bound.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:fixed-index}
Qualitative classical convergence on every fixed interval follows already
from the common contacts and Lemma~\ref{lem:reduced-specialization}.
Indeed, fix $K$ and choose a strict common contact $M>K$. Once $n>m$ and
\[(p-1)p^{n-1}=v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(p)>h(M),\]
consider an index $0\leq k\leq M$. If
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}\leq h(M)$, the lemma gives
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(b_k(\pi_{\chi_n}))
 =\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}.
\]
If instead $\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}>h(M)$, including
an identically zero reduction, the lower bound in the lemma gives
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_n}}(b_k(\pi_{\chi_n}))
 \geq\min\{\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)},e_n\}>h(M).
\]
Thus the two lists of coefficient points agree at every height at
most $h(M)$, and all their other points lie above that height. The
chord joining the common endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(M,h(M))$ bounds
both lower convex hulls above on $[0,M]$. Points above $h(M)$ cannot
affect those hulls. Finally, the common contact vertex at $M$
excludes interference from larger indices. The initial polygons agree.
The same fixed-index argument applies whenever the classical and
equal-characteristic polygons have unbounded common strict contacts, as in
the ordinary-base setting of \cite[Theorems 1.8 and 1.18]{KramerMillerUpton2023}.

In our setting $h(M)$ is quadratic, so this elementary comparison only
supplies an index range of order $p^{n/2}$. The conductor-linear range
$D_n-A$, the growing $q$-slope cutoff of
Corollary~\ref{thm:intro-left-interval}, and uniform control at arbitrary
weights require the stronger coefficient estimate of
Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-gauss}. In particular,
stability on a fixed positive $q$-slope interval is not merely fixed-index
convergence.

The reduction in \eqref{eq:limit-polygon} cannot in general be
omitted.  For example, for $r\geq1$ the series $p+T^r$ has $T$-adic order zero
before reduction, while its reduction has order $r$; its
$\pi_{\chi_n}$-adic specialization has valuation $r$ once
$(p-1)p^{n-1}>r$.  The coefficients divisible by $p$ become
irrelevant at any fixed height as $n$ grows.
This observation does not discard the higher Witt levels of the
tower, which appear at higher powers of $T$ in the reduced series.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:ordinary-criterion}
Assume eventual minimal break ratios, with $\delta=d/p^m$ as in
Definition~\ref{def:ramification-parameters}. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $p\equiv1\pmod d$;
\item $N_r$ equals the Hodge polygon for every $r>m$;
\item $N_r$ equals the Hodge polygon for at least one $r>m$.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, $m=0$, $\delta=d$, and for every $r\geq1$,
\[
 S_r=\left\{\frac{j}{dp^{r-1}}:1\leq j<dp^{r-1}\right\},
\]
with each slope occurring once. Moreover, $N_\infty$ equals the Hodge
polygon, and
\[
 N_r(k)=N_\infty(k)=h(k)=\frac{a(p-1)}{2d}k(k-1)
 \qquad(k\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0},\ r\geq1).
\]
Equality of polygons means equality of their piecewise linear graphs;
the quadratic expression $h(x)$ is used here only at integer abscissas.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We apply the finite-character Newton--Hodge equality criterion of
Kramer-Miller--Upton
\cite[Corollary 4.3 of the arXiv version]{KramerMillerUpton2023}.
This is a criterion for one finite-order character; their Theorem 1.9
states the corresponding all-character conclusion for a tower.
For a character of order $p^r$ on our tower, with Swan conductor
$s_r=\delta p^{r-1}$, it says that equality with the Hodge bound holds
precisely when $\delta$ is an integer and $p\equiv1\pmod\delta$;
the base curve $\mathbf P^1$ is already ordinary. Their normalized
local Swan conductor is $s_r/p^{r-1}=\delta=d/p^m$ in our notation.
In the $q$-adic normalization, the primitive Hodge slopes are
$j/s_r$ for $1\leq j<s_r$; multiplication by
$a(p-1)p^{r-1}$ converts them to our $v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}$ normalization. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence}, equality for this primitive
polygon is equivalent to equality for the entire characteristic polygon:
adjoining zero and repeating after integer shifts fills all Hodge slopes.

Since $p\nmid d$, the condition $\delta=d/p^m\in\mathbf Z$ forces
$m=0$. Thus (iii) implies (i). Conversely, (i) gives $d\leq p-1$.
Our reduced defining vector has $f_0\ne0$, so $\delta\geq1$; if $m>0$,
then $\delta=d/p^m<1$, a contradiction. Hence $m=0$ and the criterion
applies at every $r\geq1$, proving (ii) and the formula for $S_r$.
The implication (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) is immediate.

Finally, every integer abscissa is a strict vertex of the Hodge polygon.
At such an index $k$, the classical coefficient has valuation $h(k)$
at every level. Choose $r$ with $(p-1)p^{r-1}>h(k)$ and apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:reduced-specialization}; it forces
$\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}=h(k)$. This proves the assertion
about $N_\infty$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:rigidity-ordinarity}
In the Teichm\"uller polynomial setting, Liu--Wan call the family
\emph{rigid} when its classical characteristic polygon agrees with
the unreduced $T$-adic polygon; the transfer theorem then makes this
independent of the nontrivial finite character
\cite[Definition 2.4 and Theorem 2.3]{LiuWan2009}. Ordinarity requires
the additional equality with the Hodge polygon. Liu--Wan already
distinguish these conditions and discuss generic rigidity. The existence
results of Liu--Liu--Niu \cite{LiuLiuNiu2016} give generic rigid
one-variable polynomial families when $p>3d$. If $p\not\equiv1\pmod d$,
their common polygon is strictly above the Hodge polygon somewhere,
by Proposition~\ref{prop:ordinary-criterion}.

One must keep the two formal valuations distinct: the $T$-adic polygon
in Liu--Wan's definition is unreduced, whereas $N_\infty$ is defined
after reduction modulo $p$. Constancy of the classical polygons in a
general Witt family should not by itself be called equality with the
unreduced polygon. In particular, neither constancy of all $N_n$ nor
constancy of the normalized polygons at all nonzero weights forces
ordinarity, as the following explicit example shows.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:rigid-cubic-example}
Take $p=q=2$ and $f=[X]^3$. At the character of order two,
\[
 L_f(\chi_1,s)=1+2s^2,\qquad S_1=\{\tfrac12,\tfrac12\}.
\]
For example, the Artin--Schreier curve $y^2-y=x^3$ has three
$\mathbf F_2$-points, so its elliptic $L$-polynomial is $1+2s^2$.
By \eqref{eq:characteristic-slope-union}, the slopes of $N_1$ are
\[
 \bigsqcup_{j\geq0}\{j,j+\tfrac12,j+\tfrac12\}.
\]
We claim that $N(T_0)=N_1$ for every $0<|T_0|_2<1$, on the entire
half-line, and that $N_\infty=N_1$ as well.

Here $\pi_0(T)$ has unreduced $T$-adic order one and the splitting
product has only the degree-three factor. Applying the entry and minor
estimates of Section~\ref{sec:dwork-determinants} with $g(x)=x/3$ gives
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_T b_k(T)\geq
 \left\lceil\frac{k(k-1)}6\right\rceil.
\]
The lower convex hull of these rounded coefficient bounds is exactly
$N_1$. To check this, at $k\equiv0,1\pmod3$ the bound is the integer
$h(k)=k(k-1)/6=N_1(k)$; at $k=3r+2$ it is
$3r(r+1)/2+1$, whereas $N_1(k)=3r(r+1)/2+1/2$.
At a contact index, write
$b_k(T)=\sum_{j\geq h(k)}c_{k,j}T^j$, with $c_{k,j}\in\mathbf Z_2$;
the lower limit follows from the unreduced $T$-adic bound.
Specialization gives $v_2(b_k(-2))=h(k)$. Every term with $j>h(k)$
has valuation at least $h(k)+1$. If $c_{k,h(k)}$ were even, the term
with $j=h(k)$ would have this larger valuation as well, a contradiction.
Equivalently,
\[
 \frac{b_k(-2)}{(-2)^{h(k)}}\equiv c_{k,h(k)}\not\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
Consequently
\[
 T^{-h(k)}b_k(T)\in\mathbf Z_2[[T]]^\times
 \qquad(k\equiv0,1\pmod3).
\]
At every nonzero weight these contacts therefore have normalized height
$h(k)$. All other coefficient points remain above $N_1$ by the rounded
lower bound. This proves the claim, including its reduced version.
The quadratic lower bound also proves entireness at every such weight.

This common polygon is not the Hodge polygon: at abscissa two its
height is $1/2$, while $h(2)=1/3$. Thus even constancy at all weights,
and hence constancy on every portion of $q$-slope less than one, does
not force Hodge equality. Here ``constancy'' uses the normalized polygon
$N(T_0)$; the unnormalized $q$-slopes still scale with $v_p(T_0)$.

Although $C_1$ is supersingular, the higher curves are not. For instance,
\[
 S_2=\{\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac34,\tfrac34\},
 \qquad g(C_n)=\frac{4^n-2^n}{2}.
\]
More generally the smallest slope of $C_n$ is $2^{-n}$. These genus
values consequently do not give a sequence of supersingular curves.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:eventual-nonsupersingularity}
For a tower with eventual minimal break ratios, $C_n$ is not
supersingular for all sufficiently large $n$, whether or not $C_1$
is supersingular.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The slope-uniformity theorem of Kosters--Zhu \cite{KostersZhu2018}
applies under our attained-degree hypothesis. For any fixed
$0<\varepsilon<1/2$, it implies that $S_n$ contains a slope in
$(0,\varepsilon)$ for all sufficiently large $n$. That slope also
occurs in the zeta function of $C_n$ by \eqref{eq:curve-slope-union}.
A supersingular curve of positive genus has all its $q$-slopes equal
to $1/2$, so these curves are not supersingular. Moreover, once a level
is not supersingular, no higher level can be: its Jacobian is an
isogeny factor of every higher Jacobian, since pullback followed by
norm is multiplication by the degree of the covering.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:analytic-domain}
The series $C_f^*(T,s)$ is rigid analytic on
\begin{equation}\label{eq:analytic-domain}
 \{(T,s)\in\mathbf C_p^2:|T|_p<1,\ |s|_p<q\}.
\end{equation}
At every nontrivial classical weight $T=\chi_n(1)-1$, it is entire
as a function of $s$.  At $T=0$ it equals $1-s$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The bound \eqref{eq:uniform-gauss} is quadratic in $k$ while
$(p-1)u(k-1)\leq\delta$: in this range it reads
\[
 w_u(b_k(T))\geq\frac{a(p-1)u}{2\delta}k(k-1)=u h(k).
\]
For fixed $u>0$ and larger $k$, its summands eventually equal one,
so the resulting lower bound is linear. More explicitly,
\[
 w_u(b_k(T))\geq ak-
 a\sum_{j\geq0}\left(1-\min\left\{\frac{(p-1)uj}{\delta},1\right\}\right).
\]
The sum on the right is finite and independent of $k$.
On a product of closed discs $|T|_p\leq p^{-u}$ and
$|s|_p\leq p^v$, with $v<a$, the valuations of $b_k(T)s^k$
are therefore at least $(a-v)k$ minus this fixed finite sum.
They tend uniformly to infinity. These products cover
\eqref{eq:analytic-domain}.

At a nontrivial classical weight the product
\eqref{eq:general-C} consists of the polynomial
$(1-s)L_f(\chi_n,s)$ and its successive $q$-translates.
It converges on every bounded $s$-disc, proving entireness.
At the trivial weight $L_f(0,s)=(1-qs)^{-1}$, and
\eqref{eq:universal-C} telescopes to $1-s$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:annular-agreement}
Assume that the tower has eventual minimal break ratios, and let
$M\geq2$ satisfy $M\equiv0,1\pmod d$.
For every $T_0\in\mathbf C_p$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-contact-width}
 0<v_p(T_0)<\frac{\delta}{(p-1)(M-1)+C},
\end{equation}
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-agreement}
 N(T_0)|_{[0,M]}=N_\infty|_{[0,M]}.
\end{equation}
The first $M$ slopes of the unnormalized polygon
$\operatorname{NP}_{v_p}C_f^*(T_0,s)$ are strictly less than $a$.
Equivalently, the corresponding slopes of $N(T_0)$ are less
than $a/v_p(T_0)$, so their zeros all belong to $|s|_p<q$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{def:boundary-annulus}
For an integer $K\geq1$, put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annulus-width}
 \varepsilon_K=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\frac{\delta}{(p-1)(K+d-2)+C},&d\geq2,\\[4pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{\delta}{(p-1)K},&d=1,
 \end{cases}\qquad
 \mathscr W_K=\{T\in\mathbf C_p:0<v_p(T)<\varepsilon_K\}.
\end{equation}
Thus $\mathscr W_K$ is the annulus
$p^{-\varepsilon_K}<|T|_p<1$, and $\varepsilon_K$ is its width
in the valuation coordinate.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:annulus-width}
For every $T_0\in\mathscr W_K$, the polygons $N(T_0)$ and
$N_\infty$ agree on $[0,K]$.  In fact the same bound gives
agreement through $K+1$, with all those roots in $|s|_p<q$.
In particular
\[
 \varepsilon_K\sim\frac{\delta}{(p-1)K}\qquad(K\longrightarrow\infty).
\]
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Recall that $h(k)=a(p-1)k(k-1)/(2\delta)$ is the Hodge ordinate.
Fix a contact index $M\geq2$ and put
\[
 \tau=\frac{\delta}{(p-1)(M-1)}.
\]
For $k\leq M$ and $0\leq j<k$, we have
$(p-1)\tau j/\delta=j/(M-1)\leq1$. Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-gauss}
therefore gives
\[
 w_\tau(b_k(T))\geq
 a\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{(p-1)\tau j}{\delta}
 =\tau\frac{a(p-1)}{2\delta}k(k-1)=\tau h(k).
\]
Write $b_k(T)=\sum_jc_{k,j}T^j$.
Every nonzero term then satisfies
\[
 j+\frac{v_p(c_{k,j})}{\tau}\geq h(k).
\]
If $p\mid c_{k,j}$, integrality gives $v_p(c_{k,j})\geq1$.
Since the assumed bound on $v_p(T_0)$ implies $v_p(T_0)<\tau$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-error-gain}
 \begin{split}
 j+\frac{v_p(c_{k,j})}{v_p(T_0)}
 &\geq h(k)+v_p(c_{k,j})\left(\frac1{v_p(T_0)}-\frac1\tau\right)\\
 &\geq h(k)+\frac1{v_p(T_0)}-\frac{(p-1)(M-1)}{\delta}>h(k)+C/\delta.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Thus all terms divisible by $p$ lie above the comparison band.

Put $\nu_k=\operatorname{ord}_T\overline{b_k(T)}$.
If $\nu_k\leq h(k)+C/\delta$, the term $c_{k,\nu_k}T_0^{\nu_k}$ is the
unique term of smallest valuation: subsequent unit terms have
larger exponents, and all terms divisible by $p$ are excluded by
\eqref{eq:annular-error-gain}.  Therefore
$v_p(b_k(T_0))/v_p(T_0)=\nu_k$.
If $\nu_k>h(k)+C/\delta$, including $\nu_k=\infty$, every term lies
above that band.  Consequently every vertex of $N_\infty$ through
$M$ retains its height, and no coefficient through $M$ falls below
$N_\infty$.

We must still exclude interference from coefficients with index
greater than $M$.  Let $P_{T_0}$ join the points
\[
 \left(k,a\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\min\{\frac{(p-1)v_p(T_0)j}{\delta},1\}\right),
 \qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots,
\]
where the empty sum is zero. On $[0,M]$ this polygon is exactly
$v_p(T_0)$ times the Hodge polygon, with linear interpolation
between its integer vertices. This is a convex polygon, and \eqref{eq:uniform-gauss} places the
entire specialized coefficient polygon above it.
Since $v_p(T_0)<\tau$, its ordinate at $M$ is $v_p(T_0) h(M)$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:limit-contacts} gives $\nu_M=h(M)$, and the
preceding paragraph gives $v_p(b_M(T_0))=v_p(T_0) h(M)$.
The specialized polygon therefore touches $P_{T_0}$ at $M$.
Its incoming slope there is bounded above by
$\frac{a(p-1)v_p(T_0)}{\delta}(M-1)<a$, whereas its outgoing slope is bounded below by
$a\min\{\frac{(p-1)v_p(T_0)M}{\delta},1\}$, which is strictly larger.
These inequalities follow by comparing the two convex polygons
immediately to the left and right of their common point.
In particular $M$ is a vertex of the specialized polygon.

The lower convex hull to its left is thus determined by the first
$M+1$ coefficient points.  The same is true for $N_\infty$, which
also has a vertex at $M$.  The coefficient comparison above proves
their equality on $[0,M]$ after division by $v_p(T_0)$.
Finally the last slope of $N_\infty$ before $M$ is at most
$h(M)-h(M-1)=a\frac{(p-1)(M-1)}{\delta}$.  The corresponding $v_p$-slope after specialization at $T_0$ is strictly less than $a$, so all these $M$ roots belong to $|s|_p<q$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Choose the least contact index $M>K$. For $d\geq2$, the contact
residues are zero and one modulo $d$, so
\[
 K+1\leq M\leq K+d-1,\qquad M-1\leq K+d-2.
\]
Indeed, if $K$ has residue zero, the next integer is a contact;
otherwise the next multiple of $d$ is at most $K+d-1$.
For $d=1$ every integer is a contact, so $M=K+1$ and $C=0$.
In both cases $M\geq2$.
The bound $v_p(T_0)<\varepsilon_K$ implies
$1/v_p(T_0)>\frac{(p-1)(M-1)}{\delta}+C/\delta$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:annular-agreement} gives
agreement through $M$ and in particular through $K+1$.
Its final assertion also places those first $K+1$ roots in the
common analytic domain.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:weight-radius-bound}
For every nonzero weight $T_0$ in the open unit disc,
\[
 R(T_0)\geq
 \max\left\{1,\frac{\delta}{(p-1)v_p(T_0)}-\frac C{p-1}-d+1\right\}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
We already know from Proposition~\ref{prop:analytic-domain} that
$C_f^*(0,s)=1-s$. Hence $b_1(T)\in-1+T\mathbf Z_p[[T]]$, so $b_1(T_0)$
is a unit at every weight in the open unit disc. All coefficients are
integral, and the initial segment from abscissa zero to one is therefore
horizontal, both after specialization and after reduction. Thus
$R(T_0)\geq1$. This lower bound is useful even for nonzero weights:
the other expression in the maximum can be less than one.

Solving the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:annular-agreement} for $M$
gives
\[
 M<\frac{\delta}{(p-1)v_p(T_0)}-\frac{C}{p-1}+1.
\]
Choose the largest multiple $M$ of $d$ strictly below this upper bound.
Consecutive multiples of $d$ are $d$ apart, so
\[
 M\geq\frac{\delta}{(p-1)v_p(T_0)}-\frac{C}{p-1}-d+1.
\]
If this lower bound exceeds one, then $M\geq2$ and the theorem gives
$R(T_0)\geq M$. Otherwise the bound $R(T_0)\geq1$ suffices.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:annular-fixed-interval}
Assume eventual minimal break ratios.  For $0<c<1$, every weight satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-interval-annulus}
 0<v_p(T)<\frac{\delta(1-c)}{C+(p-1)d}
\end{equation}
has the exact multiset identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-interval-slopes}
 \operatorname{Slopes}_q C_f^*(T,s)\cap[0,c)
 =\left(\frac{v_p(T)}a\operatorname{Slopes}N_\infty\right)\cap[0,c).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
