We give the additional calculation to justify that assertion.

Use the null vectors $\lambda_i,\rho_i$ and bridges $\mathbf B_{i,j}$
of Section~\ref{sec:cofactor-principle}. The added level-zero monomial
has the same excess $1/4$ as the tails. Its bridge, before multiplying
by its coefficient two, is
\[
 \mathbf B_{i,0}=(e_{7u-v})_{0\leq u,v\leq7^{i-1}}.
\]
The support of $\rho_i$ and the Artin--Hasse recurrence give
\[
 (\mathbf B_{i,0}\rho_i)_u
 =e_{7u}+\sum_{b=0}^{i-1}e_{7u-7^b}
 =e_{7u}-\mathbf1_{\{u=7^{i-1}\}}.
\]
Indeed the sum over all $b\geq0$ vanishes; among its omitted terms,
only $b=i$, $u=7^{i-1}$ can contribute. The vector $(e_{7u})_u$
is a column of $\mathbf C_i$, annihilated by $\lambda_i^T$, and
$\lambda_i$ has last coordinate one. Thus
\[
 \lambda_i^T\mathbf B_{i,0}\rho_i=-1,
 \qquad
 2\lambda_i^T\mathbf B_{i,0}\rho_i+
 \sum_{1\leq j<n}\lambda_i^T\mathbf B_{i,j}\rho_i
 =-2+2\mathbf1_{\{n>i\}}.
\]
For $i\geq2$, this is nonzero at level $i$ and zero at every higher
level. The residue dictionary therefore gives coefficient heights
$h(K_i)+1/4$ at level $i$ and at least $h(K_i)+1/2$ afterward.
Two tail occurrences cost at least $1/2$, a noninitial minor costs
at least $3/4$, and the parameter and coefficient errors are larger;
thus none interferes with the tested excess $1/4$.
Every chord across the integer $K_i$ has height at least
$h(K_i)+3/8$, by \eqref{eq:chord-identity}. Consequently
\[
 N_i(K_i)=h(K_i)+\frac14,
 \qquad N_n(K_i)\geq h(K_i)+\frac38\quad(n>i).
\]
The same lower bound holds for $N_\infty(K_i)$. This gives an upward
change and again $R_i=D_i+1$ for $i\geq2$. Together with the downward
changes of the preceding family, it shows that no general monotonicity
in the conductor should be imposed on the sequence $N_n$.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:positive-loss}
Consider the $\mathbf Z_7$-tower over $\mathbf F_7$ defined by
\[
 f=[X]^{11}+\sum_{j\geq2}7^j[X]^{11\cdot7^j-19}.
\]
Then $D_n=11\cdot7^{n-1}$ and $h(k)=3k(k-1)/11$.
For every $n\geq2$, at $K=D_n-4$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-witness}
 N_n(K)=h(K)+\frac{72}{11},\qquad
 N_{n+1}(K)\leq h(K)+\frac{61}{11}.
\end{equation}
The same upper bound at $K$ holds for $N_\infty(K)$.
Both $N_{n+1}(x)$ and $N_\infty(x)$ lie strictly below $N_n(x)$
throughout $(D_n-10,D_n)$. Together with the agreement through
$D_n-10$ supplied by Corollary~\ref{cor:degree-eleven-loss}, this gives
\[
 R_n=D_n-10\qquad(n\geq2).
\]
Thus eventual minimal break ratios do not force agreement with
the limit on the entire first characteristic block.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:loss-square-blocks}
For every $t\geq0$ and $0\leq c\leq6$, the square matrix
\[
 (e_{7u-v+c})_{0\leq u,v<t}
\]
is invertible over $\mathbf F_7$. The determinant of the empty
matrix is interpreted as one.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
This is the contact-block argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:contact-blocks},
now applied to the monomial tower $[X]^{11}$ and residues modulo eleven.
At its contact index $11t$, every noninitial principal minor has strictly
positive excess over the Hodge bound. Thus the leading initial matrix
has nonzero determinant modulo seven. Group rows by a residue
$a\in\{0,\ldots,10\}$ and pair them with columns of residue
$7a\bmod11$, represented in $\{0,\ldots,10\}$. Its square blocks are
\[
 (e_{7u-v+\lfloor7a/11\rfloor})_{0\leq u,v<t}.
\]
Their determinant product, up to sign, is nonzero. The shifts
$\lfloor7a/11\rfloor$ run through $0,\ldots,6$, so every stated
matrix is invertible. These are also the matrices occurring among the
contact blocks in the characteristic-seven case of
Lemma~\ref{lem:contact-blocks};
only their grouping by residues has changed.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:degree-eleven-monomial}
For the monomial tower $[X]^{11}$ over $\mathbf F_7$, every classical
characteristic polygon, and its reduced limiting polygon, is the Hodge
contact polygon for $h(k)=3k(k-1)/11$. Its slopes are
\[
 \bigsqcup_{j\geq0}
 \{6j,\ \underbrace{6j+3,\ldots,6j+3}_{10\text{ times}}\}.
\]
In particular its segment on $[1,11]$ is $y=3(x-1)$, and its
maximum excess above $h$ is $75/11$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
The entry with original
row and column indices $u,v$ in its leading residue matrix is
$e_{(7u-v)/11}$ if $v\equiv7u\pmod{11}$, and is zero otherwise.
Thus a row of residue $a$ can meet only a column of residue $7a$.
Multiplication by seven has the single cycle
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-residue-cycle}
 1\longmapsto7\longmapsto5\longmapsto2\longmapsto3
 \longmapsto10\longmapsto4\longmapsto6\longmapsto9
 \longmapsto8\longmapsto1
\end{equation}
on the ten nonzero residues modulo eleven.

Let $I$ be the common row and column index set of a principal submatrix.
If its determinant is nonzero, some permutation term is nonzero. That
term matches every selected row to a distinct selected column, with a row
of residue $a$ matched to a column of residue $7a$. Consequently
\[
 \#\{u\in I:u\equiv a\pmod{11}\}
 =\#\{u\in I:u\equiv7a\pmod{11}\}.
\]
Following the cycle shows that all ten nonzero residue classes have the
same count. The zero-residue count can be different.

The same residue restriction holds before reduction: the splitting
series is $E(\pi_0(T)X^{11})$, so its coefficients vanish in degrees
not divisible by eleven. For either a classical specialization or the
reduced universal series, every nonzero determinant term has valuation
at least $\frac6{11}\sum_{u\in I}u$.
For a classical character of order $7^r$, an integral coefficient
divisible by seven contributes an additional valuation of at least
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(7)=\varphi(7^r)=6\cdot7^{r-1}.
\]
Indeed $v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}(\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_r}))=1$, so
$\pi_0(\pi_{\chi_r})^m a$ with $a\in7\mathbf Z_7$ has valuation
at least $m+6\cdot7^{r-1}$. Such coefficients vanish in the reduced
series, and at classical characters only increase the lower bound.
Thus it suffices to bound the index sum, without assuming that every
Artin--Hasse coefficient is a unit.

Denote the common count in each nonzero residue class by $t$, and let $z$
be the number of selected indices divisible by eleven. Thus the size is
$k=z+10t$. The smallest possible index sum is
\[
 \sum_{v=0}^{z-1}11v+
 \sum_{b=1}^{10}\sum_{v=0}^{t-1}(11v+b)
 =\frac{11z(z-1)}2+55t^2.
\]
Multiplying by $6/11$ and subtracting $h(k)$ gives
\[
 3z(z-1)+30t^2-h(z+10t)
 =\frac{30(z-t)(z-t-1)}{11}.
\]
The difference $z-t$ is congruent to $k$ modulo eleven.
For example, when $k=10$, the choice $t=1$, $z=0$ has minimum
index sum $1+\cdots+10=55$ and hence valuation at least
$(6/11)\cdot55=30>3(10-1)$. The alternative $t=0$, $z=10$
has an even larger lower bound. The following comparison treats every
size at once.

To compare this with the contact polygon, write $k=11j+r$ with
$1\leq r\leq11$. The contact chord from $11j+1$ to $11j+11$ has
excess over $h(k)$ equal to
\[
 \frac3{11}(r-1)(11-r).
\]
Among all integers congruent to $r$ modulo eleven, the quadratic
$u(u-1)$ is minimized at one of $u=r$ and $u=r-11$.
For these two possibilities the desired comparison follows from
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 30r(r-1)-3(r-1)(11-r)&=33(r-1)^2\geq0,\\
 30(r-11)(r-12)-3(r-1)(11-r)&=33(11-r)^2\geq0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus every coefficient point lies on or above the contact chord.
The possible restriction $z,t\geq0$ only increases this lower bound.
The common contacts at $k\equiv0,1\pmod{11}$, including the initial
contact at zero, force equality with the contact polygon.

The segment from $11j$ to $11j+1$ has slope
$h(11j+1)-h(11j)=6j$ and length one. The next segment, from $11j+1$
to $11j+11$, has slope $6j+3$ and length ten. This proves the
stated slope list.
Its maximum excess over $h$ is $75/11$.

The contact equalities used here hold for every classical conductor
and for the reduced limiting polygon. The argument therefore proves
both assertions at once.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:loss-first-block}
For the tower in Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-loss} and every $r\geq2$,
\[
 N_r(x)=3(x-1)\qquad(1\leq x\leq11).
\]
Consequently, for $n\geq2$ and $K=D_n-4$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-old-height}
 N_n(K)=h(K)+\frac{72}{11}.
\end{equation}
The entire interval $[D_n-10,D_n]$ is one straight segment of $N_n$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-eleven-monomial}, the monomial polygon
on $[1,11]$ is the chord $y=3(x-1)$, whose excess above $h$ is
\[
 3(k-1)-h(k)=\frac3{11}(k-1)(11-k)\leq\frac{75}{11}.
\]
We next restore the higher Witt terms of the tower in
Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-loss}. They all have level at least two, so
$f^{<2}=[X]^{11}$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:tail-estimate} with truncation
level two and arbitrary character level $r\geq2$. Since
$p=7$, $\delta=11$, and $D_2=77$, it gives
\[
 v_{\pi_{\chi_r}}\bigl(b_k(f,\pi_{\chi_r})-b_k([X]^{11},\pi_{\chi_r})\bigr)
 \geq h(k)+\frac{6(77-k+1)+1}{11}.
\]
For $1\leq k\leq11$, the added quantity is at least $403/11$, which
is strictly larger than the maximum chord excess $75/11$. Hence every
coefficient perturbation lies strictly above $3(k-1)$. The original
coefficient points on or above the chord remain on or above it. At
$k=1,11$, the perturbation has strictly higher valuation and preserves
the contact height. Taking the lower convex hull therefore preserves
the whole segment. This proves $N_r(x)=3(x-1)$ on $[1,11]$.

Finally, the reflected-excess identity \eqref{eq:reflected-excess} says
\[
 N_n(k)-h(k)=N_n(D_n-k+1)-h(D_n-k+1).
\]
It expresses slope symmetry after accounting for the initial zero slope
of the characteristic series. At $K=D_n-4$, the reflected index is
$D_n-K+1=5$. Since $N_n(5)=12$ and $h(5)=60/11$, we obtain
\[
 N_n(K)-h(K)=N_n(5)-h(5)=12-\frac{60}{11}=\frac{72}{11}.
\]
Reflection sends $[1,11]$ to $[D_n-10,D_n]$. Substitution throughout
that interval gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 N_n(x)&=h(x)-h(D_n-x+1)+3(D_n-x)\\
 &=h(D_n)+\left(\frac{6D_n}{11}-3\right)(x-D_n).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The expression is linear. The identity at integer points extends across
the interval because Newton polygon vertices have integer abscissas.
This proves the last assertion.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:loss-index-set}
Let $L\geq6$ be an integer, $K=11L-4$, and $\ell=77L-19$.
Consider the matrix
\[
 \left([X^{7u-v}]\,\overline E(X^{11})(1+zX^\ell)\right)_{u,v\geq0}
\]
over $\mathbf F_7[z]$. Among its size-$K$ principal minors whose index
excess is at most seven, only the index set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-index-set}
 I=\{0,\ldots,11L-8\}\cup\{11L-6,11L-4,11L-1\}
\end{equation}
can have a nonzero coefficient of $z$. Its excess is seven.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
A term linear in $z$ selects one new entry and otherwise uses entries
from $\overline E(X^{11})$. Suppose the new entry has row residue $a$
and column residue $c$. Since $\ell\equiv-19\pmod{11}$,
\[
 c\equiv7a-\ell\equiv7a+8\pmod{11}.
\]
Every other selected entry sends a row residue $b$ to column residue $7b$.
We first determine which counts of indices can support such a permutation.

Write $m_b$ for the number of indices of $I$ of residue $b$.
After deleting the row and column occupied by the new entry, the remaining
matching requires
\[
 m_{7b}-\mathbf1_{\{7b=c\}}
 =m_b-\mathbf1_{\{b=a\}}\qquad(b\bmod11).
\]
At $b=0$, this excludes exactly one of $a,c$ being zero; they cannot both
be zero because $c=7a+8$. Thus both are nonzero. Along the cycle
\eqref{eq:loss-residue-cycle}, the count increases by one on entering $c$
and decreases by one on leaving $a$. It is constant elsewhere.
Hence the larger counts form the consecutive arc starting at $c$ and
ending at $a$, both endpoints included. Counts on this arc exceed those
off the arc by one.

We next restrict the zero-residue count. The initial set
$\{0,\ldots,K-1\}$ contains $L$ multiples of eleven.
To have at least $L+2$ such multiples, a set must add at least
$11L$ and $11L+11$ and remove two nonzero-residue indices no larger
than $11L-5$ and $11L-6$. Its index excess is therefore at least
\[
 11L+(11L+11)-(11L-5)-(11L-6)=22.
\]
To have at most $L-2$ multiples of eleven, it must remove two such
indices no larger than $11L-11$ and $11L-22$, while the smallest
available new nonzero indices are $11L-4$ and $11L-3$.
The excess is then at least
\[
 (11L-4)+(11L-3)-(11L-11)-(11L-22)=26.
\]
Every further replacement increases the sum. At excess at most seven,
we can therefore write $m_0=L+s$ with $s\in\{-1,0,1\}$.

There remain $10L-4-s$ nonzero indices. If the smaller nonzero count
is $t$ and the arc has length $a_0$, then
$10t+a_0=10L-4-s$, with $1\leq a_0\leq9$.
It follows that $t=L-1$ and $a_0=6-s$. Thus the larger count is $L$,
and the only possible arc lengths are five, six, and seven.

For fixed residue counts, the smallest index sum is obtained by taking
the smallest available indices in each residue class. The zero class
contributes $11(L+s)(L+s-1)/2$. Taking $L-1$ indices in each nonzero
class contributes
\[
 \sum_{b=1}^{10}\sum_{v=0}^{L-2}(11v+b)=55(L-1)^2.
\]
For each residue on the larger-count arc, one adds the index
$11(L-1)+b$. Subtracting the initial index sum gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:loss-prefix-excess}
\begin{aligned}
 E_{\min}
 &=\frac{11}{2}(L+s)(L+s-1)+55(L-1)^2
   +11(L-1)(6-s)\\
 &\hspace{1.5em}+\sum_{b\text{ on the arc}}b
   -\frac{(11L-4)(11L-5)}2\\
 &=\sum_{b\text{ on the arc}}b-21+\frac{11}{2}s(s+1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In particular the dependence on $L$ cancels.

For completeness, the allowed new row residues
$a=1,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10$ give arc lengths
$5,4,3,8,1,9,2,7,6$, respectively. The row residue $2$ is excluded
because its new column has residue zero. Keeping only lengths five,
six, and seven leaves the following three possibilities:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccccl@{}}
\toprule
New row & New column & $s$ & $E_{\min}$ & Larger-count arc\\
\midrule
$1$ & $4$ & $1$ & $18$ & $4,6,9,8,1$\\
$9$ & $5$ & $-1$ & $18$ & $5,2,3,10,4,6,9$\\
$10$ & $1$ & $0$ & $7$ & $1,7,5,2,3,10$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For example, the last arc has residue sum $28$, giving $28-21=7$.
Changing any initial segment within a fixed residue class raises the
index sum by at least eleven. Therefore only the last row of the table,
with the smallest indices in each class, can occur at excess at most
seven. Those indices are exactly \eqref{eq:loss-index-set}.
Relative to $\{0,\ldots,11L-5\}$, this set removes
$11L-7,11L-5$ and adds $11L-4,11L-1$, for a net excess of seven.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
<!-- proof-76: body_md -->
For part (i), Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-loss} gives a difference between
$N_n$ and $N_{n+1}$ at $D_n-4<D_n$ for every $n\geq2$.
If the first-block multiset identity held, Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-block-stability}
with $b=1$ would give equality on $[0,D_n]$, contradicting this point
of difference. Thus the first-block identity fails at every such level.
For part (ii), Proposition~\ref{prop:complete-not-strong} proves agreement
through $D_n+1$ and a difference at $D_n+2<2D_n$ for every $n\geq2$.
Agreement through $D_n$ gives the first-block identity by the same
criterion with $b=1$. If the two-block identity held, the criterion with
$b=2$ would give equality through $2D_n$, contradicting the difference
at $D_n+2$. Thus complete first-block propagation holds while two-block
propagation fails.
The ramification assertions were verified for each example above.
<!-- end proof-76 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:annular-failure}
Over $\mathbf F_7$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-witt-vector}
 n_1=2,\qquad n_{r+1}=11\cdot7^{n_r-1},\qquad
 f=[X]^{11}+\sum_{r\geq1}7^{n_r}[X]^{11\cdot7^{n_r}-96}.
\end{equation}
This tower has minimal breaks $D_n=11\cdot7^{n-1}$.
Its degree gap is $96$, whereas the sufficient constant in
\eqref{eq:intro-gap} is $75$. Every classical polygon is the same
as for the monomial tower $[X]^{11}$, so the tower is slope stable.
Its limiting polygon is the Hodge contact polygon, with slopes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-limit-slopes}
 \bigsqcup_{j\geq0}
 \{6j,\ \underbrace{6j+3,\ldots,6j+3}_{10\text{ times}}\}.
\end{equation}
Nevertheless, for every $n=n_r$ there is a weight $T_0$ with
\[
 v_7(T_0)=\frac{11}{6(D_n-13)}
\]
such that, at $K=D_n-15$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-failure-height}
 N(T_0)(K)\leq h(K)+\frac{60}{11}
 <h(K)+\frac{72}{11}=N_\infty(K).
\end{equation}
The limiting segment containing $K$ specializes to slope
$1-7/(2(D_n-13))<1$.
Thus \eqref{eq:full-annular-law} fails on every boundary annulus,
although $R_n=\infty$ for every classical level $n\geq1$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:annular-monomial}
For the tower \eqref{eq:annular-witt-vector}, every classical
characteristic polygon and the limiting polygon equal the monomial
polygon of Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-eleven-monomial}. Their slopes are
\eqref{eq:annular-limit-slopes}.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-77: body_md -->
The monomial polygon has maximum excess $75/11$ over $h$.
In the reduced universal series, a tail monomial at level $n_r$ has
weighted order
\[
 7^{n_r}-\frac{11\cdot7^{n_r}-96}{11}=\frac{96}{11}.
\]
Every term in the difference of a full Fredholm coefficient and its
monomial counterpart uses at least one tail occurrence. Its principal
index sum contributes at least $h(k)$, so the difference has valuation
at least $h(k)+96/11$, strictly above the monomial polygon.
Its contact vertices are therefore preserved, and no other coefficient
point can fall below it. This proves equality of the limiting polygons.

At a finite character of order $7^m$, each active tail has level
$n_r<m$ and parameter valuation $7^{n_r}$; inactive tails vanish.
The weighted order of each active tail is again $96/11$.
The same coefficient comparison preserves the entire monomial polygon
at every conductor. Thus every normalized classical polygon equals
the limiting polygon, and Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence}
gives slope stability.
<!-- end proof-77 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:annular-effective-gap}
At this weight,
\[
 v_{T_0}\left(\frac{\pi_i(T_0)}{\pi_0(T_0)^{7^i}}-1\right)
 \geq\frac{318}{11}\quad(0\leq i<n),
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-new-parameter}
 v_{T_0}\left(\frac{\pi_n(T_0)}{7\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}}-1\right)
 \geq\frac{77}{11}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $\ell=11\cdot7^n-96$,
\[
 v_{T_0}(\pi_n(T_0))-\frac\ell{11}=\frac{18}{11}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-78: body_md -->
Evaluate the formal congruence
$\pi_i(T)-\pi_0(T)^{7^i}\in7T\mathbf Z_7[[T]]$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:pi-congruence} at $T=T_0$, and divide by
$\pi_0(T_0)^{7^i}$. For $i<n$ this gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 v_{T_0}\left(\frac{\pi_i(T_0)}{\pi_0(T_0)^{7^i}}-1\right)
 &\geq v_{T_0}(7)+1-7^i\\
 &\geq\frac{6(D_n-13)+11-D_n}{11}
 =\frac{5D_n-67}{11}\geq\frac{318}{11},
 \end{aligned}
\]
since $D_n\geq77$. For $i=0$ the difference is zero and its valuation
is infinite. In particular $\pi_{n-1}(T_0)$ has valuation $D_n/11$,
and its ratio to $\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}$ is one to the stated precision.

Put $y(T_0)=E(\pi_{n-1}(T_0))-1$. The defining identities give
\[
 E(\pi_n(T_0))-1=(1+y(T_0))^7-1
 =7y(T_0)+\sum_{j=2}^{6}\binom7j y(T_0)^j+y(T_0)^7.
\]
Here $v_{T_0}(y(T_0))=D_n/11$, because
$E(U)-1=U+O(U^2)$ preserves positive valuations and
$v_{T_0}(\pi_{n-1}(T_0))=D_n/11$.
The first term has valuation
\[
 v_{T_0}(7y(T_0))=\frac{6(D_n-13)+D_n}{11}
 =\frac{7D_n-78}{11}.
\]
For $2\leq j\leq6$, the coefficient $\binom7j$ has seven-adic
valuation one, so its term is higher than $7y(T_0)$ by
$(j-1)D_n/11\geq77/11$. The last term is higher by
\[
 v_{T_0}(y(T_0)^7)-v_{T_0}(7y(T_0))=\frac{78}{11}.
\]
Also, replacing $y(T_0)$ by $\pi_{n-1}(T_0)$ in $7y(T_0)$ introduces a relative error of
valuation at least $D_n/11\geq77/11$.

Applying \eqref{eq:pi-first-two-terms} at $j=n$ and $T=T_0$ gives
\[
 \pi_n(T_0)=(1+T_0)^{7^n}-1
       +O\!\left(\bigl((1+T_0)^{7^n}-1\bigr)^2\right).
\]
This inverse substitution introduces a relative error of valuation
at least $v_{T_0}((1+T_0)^{7^n}-1)=(7D_n-78)/11>77/11$.
Combining these estimates, and finally replacing $\pi_{n-1}(T_0)$ by
$\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}$, proves \eqref{eq:annular-new-parameter}.
The leading term is consequently $7\pi_0(T_0)^{7^{n-1}}$, with valuation
$(7D_n-78)/11$. Subtracting $\ell/11=(7D_n-96)/11$ gives $18/11$.
<!-- end proof-78 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{prop:annular-coefficient}
The finite head satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-coefficient}
 v_{T_0}\bigl(b_K(f^{\leq n},T_0)\bigr)=h(K)+\frac{60}{11}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-79: body_md -->
We first exclude every contribution below the claimed height except
one possible principal determinant. For a size-$K$ index set $I$, put
$E_I=\sum_{u\in I}u-K(K-1)/2$. As in Section~\ref{sec:loss-coefficient}, a term with
$b$ new tail occurrences has expected weighted excess
\[
 \frac{6E_I+18b}{11}.
\]
The actual excess is at least this quantity; a nonzero leading
residue gives equality. We must control the full determinant sum,
not just produce one low term: a second principal minor at the same
height could cancel it. We first exclude $b=0$ and $b\geq2$,
then use the residue-count lemma to isolate the index set for $b=1$.
The following estimates account for all nonnegative integers $b$.

\emph{No new occurrence.} If $b=0$, the determinant comes from the
monomial matrix. Here $K\equiv7\pmod{11}$. In the count calculation
of Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-eleven-monomial}, the smallest value of
$30u(u-1)/11$ with $u\equiv7\pmod{11}$ is attained at $u=-4$ and
is $600/11$. Seven-divisible terms have excess at least $384/11$.
Neither kind contributes through excess $60/11$.

\emph{At least two new occurrences.} A matrix entry containing one
occurrence must have $7u-v\geq\ell$, and $v\geq0$, so its row is
at least
\[
 u\geq\left\lceil\frac{7D_n-96}{7}\right\rceil=D_n-13.
\]
The largest index of the initial set is $K-1=D_n-16$.
Thus even one occurrence forces $E_I\geq3$.
If $b=2$ and the occurrences lie in different entries, their row indices
are distinct and at least $D_n-13,D_n-12$. Compared with the two largest
initial indices $D_n-16,D_n-17$, their excess is at least
\[
 (D_n-13)+(D_n-12)-(D_n-16)-(D_n-17)=8.
\]
Their weighted excess is at least $(6\cdot8+18\cdot2)/11=84/11$.
If both lie in the same entry, its row is at least
$\lceil2\ell/7\rceil=2D_n-27$. Then
$E_I\geq(2D_n-27)-(D_n-16)=D_n-11\geq66$, which costs still more.
For $b=3$, excess at most $60/11$ would force $E_I\leq1$, contrary
to $E_I\geq3$. For $b\geq4$, the tail contribution alone is at least
$72/11$. This excludes every case with $b\geq2$.

\emph{Exactly one new occurrence.} Now $b=1$, and excess at most
$60/11$ requires $E_I\leq7$. Lemma~\ref{lem:loss-index-set}, applied
with its local parameter $L=7^{n-1}-1$, leaves precisely
\[
 I=\{0,\ldots,D_n-19\}\cup\{D_n-17,D_n-15,D_n-12\}.
\]
Its excess is seven, so its contribution has exactly the required
weighted order $(6\cdot7+18)/11=60/11$.

We must prove that this one contribution is nonzero. Its residue counts
have the same pattern as in Section~\ref{app:positive-loss}, with each
block size reduced by one. The exceptional blocks are
\[
 \mathbf C=(e_{7u-v+6})_{\substack{0\leq u<7^{n-1}-1\\0\leq v<7^{n-1}-2}},
 \qquad
 \mathbf D=(e_{7u-v+5})_{\substack{0\leq u<7^{n-1}-2\\0\leq v<7^{n-1}-1}}.
\]
All other blocks are square and invertible, and deleting the last row
of $\mathbf C$ or last column of $\mathbf D$ leaves an invertible square block by
Lemma~\ref{lem:loss-square-blocks}. Therefore the full leading matrix
has corank one. Normalize the left null vector $\lambda$ of $\mathbf C$ to
have last coordinate one. Its existence and normalization follow as in
the preceding example.

The shortened wide block $\mathbf D$ requires a different right null vector.
We construct it explicitly from the Artin--Hasse recurrence. The
row equations ask for a polynomial $\rho(X)$ such that
$\overline E(X)\rho(X)$ has zero coefficients in degrees $7u+5$
over the required range. The operator $X\,d/dX-5$ kills precisely
these coefficients in characteristic seven. We therefore seek a
Laurent polynomial $Q(X)$ for which applying this operator to
$Q(X)\overline E(X)$ produces $\overline E(X)$ times a series
that can be truncated to the desired polynomial. This explains
the following finite construction. All its coefficients lie in
$\mathbf F_7$. Put
\[
 P(X)=4+X+5X^2+6X^3+6X^4+X^5,\qquad
 Q(X)=X^{-9}-X^{-8}+X^{-7}P(X).
\]
The Laurent polynomial $Q$ has terms of degrees $-9$ through $-2$.
A direct finite calculation gives
\[
 Q(X)(X+X^7)-5Q(X)+XQ'(X)=P(X).
\]
For example, the coefficient of a negative power $X^j$ on the left
is the sum of $(j-5)[X^j]Q$, $[X^{j-1}]Q$, and $[X^{j-7}]Q$;
these sums vanish for every negative $j$. The remaining coefficients
in degrees zero through five are $4,1,5,6,6,1$.
Adding the remaining terms of the Artin--Hasse series yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-null-identity}
 Q(X)\sum_{j\geq0}X^{7^j}-5Q(X)+XQ'(X)
 =P(X)+\sum_{j\geq2}X^{7^j}Q(X).
\end{equation}

The differential form of \eqref{eq:loss-AH-recurrence} is
$X\overline E'(X)=\overline E(X)\sum_{j\geq0}X^{7^j}$.
After multiplying \eqref{eq:annular-null-identity} by $\overline E(X)$,
the left side becomes
\[
 \left(X\frac{d}{dX}-5\right)\bigl(Q(X)\overline E(X)\bigr).
\]
Its coefficient of $X^m$ is $(m-5)[X^m](Q\overline E)$, which is
zero whenever $m\equiv5\pmod7$. Thus the product of
$\overline E(X)$ with the right side of \eqref{eq:annular-null-identity}
has zero coefficients at all such exponents.

Define the finite polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-null-polynomial}
 \rho(X)=P(X)+\sum_{j=2}^{n-1}X^{7^j}Q(X)
 =\sum_{v=0}^{7^{n-1}-2}\rho_vX^v.
\end{equation}
For $n=2$ the sum is empty and $\rho=P$. In general it has degree
$7^{n-1}-2$, leading coefficient one, and $\rho_0=4$, $\rho_1=1$.
The first term omitted from the infinite series has lowest exponent
$7^n-9$. On the other hand, the row equations of $\mathbf D$ use exponents
\[
 7u+5\leq7(7^{n-1}-3)+5=7^n-16.
\]
Multiplication by $\overline E(X)$, which has only nonnegative powers,
cannot lower an omitted exponent. Hence truncation does not affect
these coefficients, and for $0\leq u<7^{n-1}-2$,
\[
 (\mathbf D\rho)_u
 =\sum_{v=0}^{7^{n-1}-2}e_{7u-v+5}\rho_v
 =[X^{7u+5}]\bigl(\overline E(X)\rho(X)\bigr)=0.
\]
This proves that the coefficient vector of \eqref{eq:annular-null-polynomial}
is the normalized right null vector of $\mathbf D$.

The new entry again connects row residue ten to column residue one.
Its block is
\[
 \mathbf B=(e_{7u-v-7^n+15})_{0\leq u,v<7^{n-1}-1}.
\]
Indeed its entry is obtained by subtracting $\ell=11\cdot7^n-96$
from $7(11u+10)-(11v+1)$ and dividing by eleven.
For $u\leq7^{n-1}-3$, the coefficient index is negative.
At the last row $u=7^{n-1}-2$, it is $1-v$.
Thus only that last row is nonzero and it is $(1,1,0,\ldots,0)$.
The resulting cofactor pairing is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-pairing}
 \lambda^T\mathbf B\rho=\rho_0+\rho_1=5\ne0\quad\text{in }\mathbf F_7.
\end{equation}
As before, the cofactors are a fixed nonzero scalar times the products
of the extended left and right null-vector coordinates. The coefficient
linear in the new term is therefore this scalar times
$\lambda^T\mathbf B\rho$, and is nonzero. There is only one possible principal
index set, so no other minor can cancel it. All contributions of lower
order were excluded above, and all discarded errors have larger order.
Moreover, every term of this unique linear contribution has the same
factor $7\pi_0(T_0)^{(6\sum_{u\in I}u-\ell)/11+7^{n-1}}$.
Its remaining residue is the nonzero scalar just computed, so its
valuation is exactly its expected weight. This proves
\eqref{eq:annular-coefficient}; it is an exact coefficient valuation,
and will give an upper bound, rather than an asserted vertex height,
for the specialized Newton polygon.
<!-- end proof-79 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:witt-continuity}
If two reduced Witt equations agree modulo $p^N$, their
characteristic coefficients differ by elements of
\[
 \bigl((1+T)^{p^N}-1\bigr)\mathbf Z_p[[T]].
\]
This also holds for an equation obtained as the limit of its Witt
truncations.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-80: body_md -->
Work in the complete noetherian local ring $\mathbf Z_p[[T]]$, with its
$(p,T)$-adic topology. At a closed point, the two Frobenius exponents
differ by $p^Nz$ for some $z\in\mathbf Z_p$, because the defining equations
agree modulo $p^N$ and the trace preserves this divisibility.
The difference of the character values is therefore a unit power of
$1+T$ times $(1+T)^{p^Nz}-1$.

To see the required divisibility integrally, use the binomial expansion
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (1+T)^{p^Nz}-1
 &=\left(1+\bigl((1+T)^{p^N}-1\bigr)\right)^z-1\\
 &=\bigl((1+T)^{p^N}-1\bigr)
   \sum_{j\geq1}\binom zj
      \bigl((1+T)^{p^N}-1\bigr)^{j-1}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The binomial coefficients belong to $\mathbf Z_p$, and the sum converges
$T$-adically. Thus the character values are congruent modulo the stated
principal ideal. Their Euler factors, and finite products of these
factors, are congruent modulo the same ideal. For a fixed power $s^k$,
only closed points of degree at most $k$ enter the Euler product for
$L_f^*(T,s)$. There are finitely many such points, so every $L$-coefficient
has the required congruence.

We must check that passing to characteristic series and infinite Witt
vectors preserves it. First,
\[
 C_f^*(T,s)=\prod_{j\geq0}L_f^*(T,q^js)
\]
converges coefficientwise: the coefficient of $s^k$ in its $j$-th
factor, for $k\geq1$, is divisible by $q^{jk}$, since the
$L$-coefficients are integral. Modulo any fixed power of $p$, all
sufficiently late factors are therefore one. This convergence is
uniform in the Witt truncation and also holds in the $(p,T)$-adic
topology.

Second, as the Witt truncation level $M$ tends to infinity,
$(1+T)^{p^M}-1$ tends to zero in that topology. One can check this
coefficientwise in each quotient by $(p,T)^d$: terms of degree at least
$d$ disappear, and for fixed positive $j<d$, the valuation of
$\binom{p^M}{j}$ tends to infinity. Hence the pointwise character values
converge, then each $L$-coefficient converges, and the uniform product
convergence gives convergence of each characteristic coefficient.
Finally every ideal of a complete noetherian local ring is closed in
its maximal-ideal topology. The ideal generated by
$(1+T)^{p^N}-1$ is therefore closed, so both limits retain the congruence.
<!-- end proof-80 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:uniform-partial}
For every $n>m$ such that $D_n>A_{\mathrm u}$ and every $r\geq n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-polygon-agreement}
 N_r|_{[0,D_n-A_{\mathrm u}+1]}
 =N_n|_{[0,D_n-A_{\mathrm u}+1]}
 =N_\infty|_{[0,D_n-A_{\mathrm u}+1]}.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-primitive-agreement}
 S_r\cap\left(0,\frac{D_n-A_{\mathrm u}}{D_r}\right)
 =(p^{n-r}S_n)\cap\left(0,\frac{D_n-A_{\mathrm u}}{D_r}\right),
\end{equation}
and each side contains exactly $D_n-A_{\mathrm u}-1$ slopes,
with multiplicity.
In particular, the only starting conditions are $n>m$ and
$d p^{n-m-1}>A_{\mathrm u}$, both independent of $a$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:uniform-gap}
Suppose $d\geq3$ and that, for an integer $N>m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-tail-gap}
 \deg f_i\leq\delta p^i-C_{\mathrm u}\qquad(i\geq N).
\end{equation}
If $N\geq2$, let $n_0\geq N$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-start}
 p^{n_0-1}\geq p^{N-2}
       +\frac1{2\delta}\left\lfloor\frac{(d-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
If $N=1$, then $m=0$, and the first term on the right is omitted:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-polynomial-start}
 p^{n_0-1}\geq
       \frac1{2d}\left\lfloor\frac{(d-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad n_0\geq1.
\end{equation}
Then $N_n=N_\infty$ on the entire half-line for every $n\geq n_0$.
The tower is slope stable with starting level $n_0$.

If $d\leq2$, no degree-gap hypothesis is needed: $N_n=N_\infty$
for every $n>m$, and the tower is slope stable from level $m+1$.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- corollary-22: body_md -->
\label{cor:uniform-small-degree}
If $1\leq d\leq6$, then $R_n\geq D_n+1$ for every $n>m$.
Thus the first block propagates completely to every higher level,
over every $\mathbf F_q$ and for every prime $p$ allowed by $p\nmid d$.
<!-- end corollary-22 -->
<!-- proof-81: body_md -->
Here $\lfloor(d+1)/8\rfloor=0$, so $A_{\mathrm u}=0$.
The agreement endpoint in Theorem~\ref{thm:uniform-partial} is therefore $D_n+1$.
<!-- end proof-81 -->
<!-- corollary-23: body_md -->
\label{cor:uniform-five-example}
For the tower \eqref{eq:complete-not-strong-tower} over $\mathbf F_5$,
\[
 R_n=D_n+1\qquad(n\geq1).
\]
Complete first-block propagation holds from level one, whereas the
two-block identity fails at every level.
<!-- end corollary-23 -->
<!-- proof-82: body_md -->
Here $d=6$ and $m=0$. Corollary~\ref{cor:uniform-small-degree} gives
$R_n\geq D_n+1$ for every $n\geq1$. The active and inactive heights
in Proposition~\ref{prop:vertex} differ at $K_n=D_n+2$ for every
$n\geq1$, including $n=1$. Since vertex abscissas are integers,
the same linear-interpolation argument as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:complete-not-strong} gives equality for $R_n$.
The first-block identity follows from agreement through $D_n$,
and the two-block identity is impossible because $D_n+2<2D_n$.
<!-- end proof-82 -->
<!-- corollary-24: body_md -->
\label{cor:uniform-eleven}
For $p=q=7$ and $\delta=11$, one has $R_n\geq D_n-10$ for every
$n\geq2$. Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:positive-loss}, this recovers
the optimal universal horizontal loss ten.
<!-- end corollary-24 -->
<!-- proof-83: body_md -->
Here $m=0$, $d=11$, and $A_{\mathrm u}=11$. For $n\geq2$,
$D_n>A_{\mathrm u}$, and the agreement endpoint in
\eqref{eq:uniform-polygon-agreement} is $D_n-11+1=D_n-10$.
<!-- end proof-83 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{def:relative-precision}
The matrices $M$ and $M'$ agree to \emph{relative precision} $g\geq0$
with respect to the row weights $ci$ if
\[
 v(U_{ij}-U'_{ij})\geq g\qquad(0\leq i,j<r).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 v(M_{ij}-M'_{ij})\geq ci+g\qquad(0\leq i,j<r).
\]
Thus $g$ measures the additional agreement after the known factor
$\varpi^{ci}$ has been removed from row $i$.
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
\label{def:absolute-precision}
The matrices $M$ and $M'$ agree to \emph{absolute precision} $G\geq0$ if
\[
 v(M_{ij}-M'_{ij})\geq G\qquad(0\leq i,j<r).
\]
The same threshold is imposed on every entry, without removing its
row factor.
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:semilinear-precision}
Suppose $M=DU$ and $M'=DU'$ satisfy
\eqref{eq:semilinear-row-weights} with the same $c,r$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item If $r\geq2$, relative precision $g\geq\beta$ suffices for
$M\rho$ and $M'\rho$ to have the same slopes.
\item If $r\geq2$, absolute precision
$G\geq\beta+c(r-1)/2$ suffices, including equality.
\item For $r=1$, the normalized slope is zero and needs no
comparison; an empty block requires no assertion.
\end{enumerate}
The same conclusions hold over different coefficient fields under
the following explicit hypotheses. For a positive integer $L$, the
coefficient quotients are identified as
\[
 \mathcal O/(\varpi^L)\simeq
 \mathbf F_q[\varpi]/(\varpi^L)\simeq
 \mathcal O'/(\varpi^L),
\]
with the same uniformizer class and compatible coefficient automorphisms.
For (i), require $L\geq\lceil g\rceil$ and equality of the images of
$U,U'$ modulo $\varpi^{\lceil g\rceil}$.
For (ii), require $L\geq\lceil G\rceil$ and equality of the images of
$M,M'$ modulo $\varpi^{\lceil G\rceil}$.
No identification of the fraction fields is required.
None of these precision bounds contains $a$.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- definition-30: body_md -->
\label{def:skew-gauss-ring}
For $t\in\mathbf Q$, the \emph{skew Gauss valuation ring} is
\[
 \mathcal V_t(K)=\{x\in K(Z;\rho^{-1}):w_t(x)\geq0\},
 \qquad w_t(0)=+\infty.
\]
For an integer $L\geq1$, its truncation to precision $L$ is
$\mathcal V_t(K)/\varpi^L\mathcal V_t(K)$. Indeed $\varpi$ is central,
and
\[
 \varpi^L\mathcal V_t(K)=\{x:w_t(x)\geq L\}.
\]
Thus agreement in this quotient means that the difference has
valuation at least $L$. More generally, for a real threshold $G>0$
the truncation is
\[
 \mathcal V_t(K)\big/\{x\in\mathcal V_t(K):w_t(x)\geq G\}.
\]
The denominator is a two-sided ideal: addition preserves the lower
bound $G$, and multiplication on either side by an element of
$\mathcal V_t(K)$ adds a nonnegative valuation. Two integral elements
have the same class precisely when their difference has valuation
at least $G$. Thus the quotient records the data strictly below
precision $G$; for $G=L\in\mathbf Z_{>0}$ it is the quotient above.
<!-- end definition-30 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{prop:cyclic-semilinear-newton}
Let $K,\rho,a$ be as above, and let $F$ be an invertible
$\rho$-semilinear map on an $r$-dimensional $K$-vector space.
Suppose $e,Fe,\ldots,F^{r-1}e$ is a basis, and write
\[
 F^re=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}b_iF^ie,\qquad b_r=-1,
 \qquad \sum_{i=0}^{r}b_iF^ie=0.
\]
Then $b_0\ne0$. If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$ are the eigenvalue
valuations of $F^a$ divided by $a$, the lower convex hull of
\[
 (r-i,v(b_i))\qquad(0\leq i\leq r,\ b_i\ne0)
\]
has slopes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$, counted with horizontal
multiplicity. Equivalently, for every real $t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cyclic-slope-transform}
 \min_{0\leq i\leq r}\{v(b_i)+it\}
       =\sum_{j=1}^r\min\{\lambda_j,t\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:ore-slope-transform}
For every rational $t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ore-slope-transform}
 w_t(\operatorname{Ddet}(M-ZI))
       =\Phi_M(t):=\sum_{j=1}^r\min\{\lambda_j,t\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-84: body_md -->
A change of semilinear basis replaces $M$ by $P^{-1}M\rho(P)$.
The inverse in \eqref{eq:ore-relation} is essential: it gives
$Z\rho(P)=PZ$ and therefore
\[
 P^{-1}M\rho(P)-ZI=P^{-1}(M-ZI)\rho(P).
\]
The two outside factors have opposite determinant valuations,
because $v(\det\rho(P))=v(\det P)$. The determinant valuation
on the left of \eqref{eq:ore-slope-transform} is thus basis independent.

We next reduce to a cyclic basis. Choose a chain of $F$-invariant
$K$-subspaces of greatest possible length,
\[
 0=V_0\subsetneq V_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_s=K^r.
\]
Such a chain exists because each strict inclusion increases dimension,
so $s\leq r$. Each quotient $V_i/V_{i-1}$ is irreducible: a nonzero
proper invariant subspace of a quotient would lift to an additional
member of the chain. Since $F$ is invertible and semilinear with
respect to an automorphism, $F(V_i)=V_i$, and the induced maps on
the quotients are invertible. This is a composition series.
In a basis adapted to it, $M$ is block triangular. The determinant
valuation is the sum for the diagonal blocks, and the slopes are
their union because $F^a$ has the same block triangular form.
No splitting of the filtration is needed.

It therefore suffices to consider an irreducible quotient. Every
nonzero vector $e$ in it is cyclic: the span of
$e,Fe,F^2e,\ldots$ is a nonzero invariant subspace, hence the whole
quotient. The first $r$ vectors are a basis, after writing $r$ for
the dimension of this quotient; otherwise their first linear
dependence would make the preceding span invariant and proper.
Write $F^re=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}b_iF^ie$ and put $b_r=-1$, as in
the proposition. In this basis, for $r\geq2$,
\[
 M-ZI=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 -Z&0&0&\cdots&0&b_0\\
 1&-Z&0&\cdots&0&b_1\\
 0&1&-Z&\cdots&0&b_2\\
 \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
 0&\cdots&0&1&-Z&b_{r-2}\\
 0&\cdots&0&0&1&b_{r-1}-Z
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Number the rows from zero. Add $\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}Z^iR_i$ to $R_0$,
with the powers of $Z$ multiplying on the left. In column $j<r-1$,
the entries cancel as $Z^j(-Z)+Z^{j+1}=0$. The new first row is
\[
 \left(0,\ldots,0,\ \sum_{i=0}^{r}Z^ib_i\right).
\]
Moving this row to the bottom gives an upper triangular matrix
with diagonal entries $1,\ldots,1$ and the displayed polynomial.
The row permutation contributes only a sign, whose valuation is zero.
For $r=1$ the matrix already consists of the scalar $b_0-Z$.
In all ranks it follows that
\[
 \begin{split}
 w_t(\operatorname{Ddet}(M-ZI))
 &=w_t\left(\sum_{i=0}^{r}Z^ib_i\right)\\
 &=\min_{0\leq i\leq r}\{v(b_i)+it\}.
 \end{split}
\]
Indeed $Z^ib_i=\rho^{-i}(b_i)Z^i$ and
$v(\rho^{-i}(b_i))=v(b_i)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:cyclic-semilinear-newton}
identifies the last minimum with $\Phi_M(t)$. Additivity over the
composition series now proves the lemma.
<!-- end proof-84 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:division-precision}
Let $B$ be an invertible integral matrix over a discretely valued
division ring, and let $\Delta$ be its determinant valuation.
Then $\Delta\geq0$, and knowing $B$ modulo valuation $P>\Delta$
determines its determinant valuation. This assertion also holds
under an isomorphism of the truncated valuation rings preserving
their valuation filtrations.

In particular, suppose two invertible integral matrices agree to
precision $P>0$ and both determinant valuations are at most $P$.
Then those valuations are equal. If both upper bounds are zero,
equality holds without any positive precision assumption.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-85: body_md -->
Move an entry of least valuation to the top left and use it to
eliminate the rest of its row and column. The required left and
right multipliers are integral, since that entry has least
valuation. Repeating gives a Smith--McMillan diagonal form by
invertible integral row and column operations. If its diagonal
valuations are $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$, then
\[
 \alpha_i\geq0,\qquad \sum_i\alpha_i=\Delta,
 \qquad \max_i\alpha_i\leq\Delta.
\]
This argument is valid over a valuation division ring; see
\cite[Propositions 3.7--3.8]{Oki2019}.

Over the same ring, the inverse of $B$ has entries of valuation
at least $-\Delta$. If $B'$ agrees with $B$ to precision
$P>\Delta$, then $B^{-1}B'=I+E$ with $E$ of positive valuation.
Its reduction is the identity, so its determinant valuation is
zero. Multiplicativity proves the assertion.

For two rings with the same truncated quotient, perform the pivot
elimination in that quotient. The first pivot and its valuation
are visible. Dividing by a pivot of valuation $\alpha$ reduces
the available precision by at most $\alpha$. After any number
of pivots, their total valuation is at most $\Delta<P$, so the
remaining pivots are still visible. Integral unit inversions and
row additions commute with the quotient isomorphism. Thus the same
pivot valuations are obtained on both sides, without identifying
the two fraction fields.

For the final assertion, if the two determinant valuations differed,
the smaller would be strictly less than $P$. Apply the assertion
just proved to the matrix with that smaller valuation. It forces the
other valuation to be equal, a contradiction. When both upper bounds
are zero, integrality makes both valuations zero. This symmetric use
of the precision lemma is what permits a non-strict threshold later.
<!-- end proof-85 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:skew-truncated-rings}
Suppose $\mathcal O/(\varpi^L)$ and $\mathcal O'/(\varpi^L)$ are
identified with $\mathbf F_q[\varpi]/(\varpi^L)$, compatibly with
coefficient automorphisms $\rho$ that fix $\varpi$. Let $t=k/e$,
where $e\geq1$ and $k\in\mathbf Z$. On both sides adjoin a central
root $u$ with $u^e=\varpi$ and $\rho(u)=u$, and write $K_e,K'_e$
for the resulting coefficient fields, with $v(u)=1/e$.
Then there is a compatible isomorphism
\[
 \mathcal V_t(K_e)/\varpi^L\mathcal V_t(K_e)
 \simeq
 \mathcal V_t(K'_e)/\varpi^L\mathcal V_t(K'_e).
\]
It preserves the valuation filtrations. For integral $t$ one may
take $e=1$, so no coefficient extension is needed.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-86: body_md -->
In both extended coefficient rings the quotient modulo $u^{eL}$
is $\mathbf F_q[u]/(u^{eL})$. This follows by adjoining the relation
$u^e=\varpi$ to the given quotients. Recall first that the original
variable has weight $w_t(Z)=t=k/e$, while $v(u)=1/e$. We remove
this weight by putting $Z=u^kW$, or $W=u^{-k}Z$. Then
\[
 w_t(W)=-k/e+t=0.
\]
Because $\rho(u)=u$, the element $u$ commutes with the coefficients
and with $Z$. The skew relation is unchanged:
\[
 Wb=u^{-k}Zb=u^{-k}\rho^{-1}(b)Z=\rho^{-1}(b)W.
\]
This substitution reduces the comparison to a variable of weight
zero, for which the Gauss valuation is simply the minimum of the
coefficient valuations. We can therefore compute the truncated
ring from the truncated coefficient ring.

Each nonzero polynomial in $W$ can be divided by its smallest
coefficient power of $u$ to become primitive, meaning that its
reduction modulo $u$ is nonzero. A primitive polynomial has Gauss
valuation zero, and its inverse belongs to the valuation ring.
Every element of that ring can be written as an integral polynomial
times the inverse of a primitive polynomial: normalize a numerator
and denominator separately and use that their valuation difference
is nonnegative.

Reducing modulo $u$ gives the residue division ring
$\mathbf F_q(W;\bar\rho^{-1})$, where $\bar\rho$ denotes the
coefficient automorphism of $\mathbf F_q$. At higher precision the
same fractions give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:common-skew-quotient}
 \mathbf F_q(W;\bar\rho^{-1})[u]/(u^{eL}).
\end{equation}
To justify this description, reduce a primitive denominator modulo
$u$. Its nonzero reduction is invertible in the residue division
ring. After factoring out this constant term, invert the remaining
expression $1+uA$ by the finite geometric series modulo $u^{eL}$.
This constructs its inverse using only the truncated coefficient
ring. Conversely, lift the numerator and denominator of each
coefficient in a polynomial in $u$ with coefficients in the residue
division ring. These two procedures are inverse, since every
primitive denominator becomes a unit and reduction to zero is
equivalent to valuation at least $L$.
The coefficient identification extends by sending the weight-zero
variable $W$ to $W$ and $u$ to $u$. Compatibility with $\rho$ ensures
that it respects $Wb=\rho^{-1}(b)W$. The powers of $u$ give the
valuation filtration, so the two identifications with
\eqref{eq:common-skew-quotient} preserve it.
A rational precision $P$ in this extension means reduction by the
ideal of elements of valuation at least $P$, equivalently by
$u^{\lceil eP\rceil}$ when $P>0$.
The argument also applies after any further common root extension.
<!-- end proof-86 -->
<!-- proof-87: body_md -->
Let $\lambda'_1,\ldots,\lambda'_r$ be the slopes of $M'\rho$, and set
\[
 \Phi_M(t)=\sum_{j=1}^r\min\{\lambda_j,t\},\qquad
 \Phi_{M'}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^r\min\{\lambda'_j,t\}.
\]
Both sets of slopes are nonnegative, because the linear $a$-th
iterates have integral matrices. Hence
$\Phi_M(t)=\Phi_{M'}(t)=rt$ for $t\leq0$. It remains to compare
these functions for rational $t>0$.

After a common root extension as above, define
\[
 Q_t=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\varpi^{-\min(ci,t)}\bigr)_{0\leq i<r}
                  (M-ZI).
\]
Since $v(M_{ij})\geq ci$ and $w_t(Z)=t$, every entry of $M-ZI$
in row $i$ has valuation at least $\min(ci,t)$. Thus all entries
of $Q_t$ lie in $\mathcal V_t$. Multiplicativity of the determinant
and Lemma~\ref{lem:ore-slope-transform} give
\[
 \begin{split}
 w_t(\operatorname{Ddet}Q_t)
 &=w_t(\operatorname{Ddet}(M-ZI))
                  -\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\min(ci,t)\\
 &=\Phi_M(t)-\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\min(ci,t).
 \end{split}
\]
The integrality of $Q_t$, together with
Lemma~\ref{lem:division-precision}, supplies nonnegativity. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalized-ore-excess}
 \Delta(t):=w_t(\operatorname{Ddet}Q_t)
       =\Phi_M(t)-\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\min(ci,t)\geq0.
\end{equation}
The same normalization defines $Q'_t$ from $M'$; its determinant
valuation $\Delta'(t)$ is nonnegative for the same reason.
The total slope of each matrix is $cr(r-1)/2$ by
\eqref{eq:semilinear-total-slope}, so
\[
 \Phi_M(t)\leq\min\left(rt,\frac{cr(r-1)}2\right).
\]
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ore-excess-majorant}
 0\leq\Delta(t),\Delta'(t)\leq q(t):=
 \min\left(rt,\frac{cr(r-1)}2\right)
                  -\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\min(ci,t).
\end{equation}
Here $q(t)$ is the auxiliary function in this display; the bare
symbol $q$ continues to denote the size of the constant field.

For $r\geq2$, $q(t)$ is strictly increasing on $[0,c(r-1)/2]$,
strictly decreasing on $[c(r-1)/2,c(r-1)]$, and zero outside
$[0,c(r-1)]$. At the unique maximum,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta-computation}
 q\left(\frac{c(r-1)}2\right)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\left(\frac{c(r-1)}2-ci\right)_+
 =\frac c2\left\lfloor\frac{r^2}{4}\right\rfloor=\beta.
\end{equation}
Here $x_+=\max(x,0)$. If $r=2s$, the midpoint is $c(s-1/2)$,
and precisely the indices $i=0,\ldots,s-1$ contribute. Their terms
are $c(s-1/2),c(s-3/2),\ldots,c/2$, whose sum is
\[
 \frac c2\bigl((2s-1)+(2s-3)+\cdots+1\bigr)=\frac{cs^2}{2}.
\]
The last equality is the sum of the first $s$ odd integers. If
$r=2s+1$, the positive terms are $cs,c(s-1),\ldots,c$, whose sum
is $cs(s+1)/2$. These give the two parity cases of
\eqref{eq:beta-computation}.

Suppose first that the matrices agree with relative precision $g$.
The corresponding matrices $Q_t,Q'_t$ then agree in row $i$ to
precision at least $g+ci-\min(ci,t)\geq g$. Since
\[
 0\leq\Delta(t),\Delta'(t)\leq q(t)\leq\beta\leq g,
\]
the symmetric assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:division-precision} gives
$\Delta(t)=\Delta'(t)$ at every rational $t>0$, including the
midpoint and the boundary value $g=\beta$. Adding back the common
row weights gives $\Phi_M(t)=\Phi_{M'}(t)$.

For absolute precision $G$, recall the normalization defining $Q_t$:
row $i$ of $M-ZI$ is divided by $\varpi^{\min(ci,t)}$.
The $-ZI$ terms are the same on the two sides, so the error in
that row has valuation at least $G-\min(ci,t)$. Uniformly in $i$
we therefore retain precision $G-\min(c(r-1),t)$. The relevant
maximum is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absolute-majorant}
 \max_t\{q(t)+\min(c(r-1),t)\}
       =\beta+\frac{c(r-1)}2\qquad(r\geq2).
\end{equation}
There is a simple way to see this without enumerating all row-weight
intervals. Cancel the last summand in the definition of $q(t)$:
\[
 q(t)+\min(c(r-1),t)
 =\min\left(rt,\frac{cr(r-1)}2\right)
       -\sum_{i=0}^{r-2}\min(ci,t).
\]
Up to the midpoint $c(r-1)/2$, the first term increases at rate
$r$, whereas the sum increases at rate at most $r-1$; thus the
difference is strictly increasing. After the midpoint the first
term is constant and the sum is nondecreasing, so the difference
is nonincreasing. Its maximum is its midpoint value, which is
$\beta+c(r-1)/2$ by \eqref{eq:beta-computation}.

If $G\geq\beta+c(r-1)/2$, this maximum calculation gives
\[
 G-\min(c(r-1),t)\geq q(t)\geq\Delta(t),\Delta'(t)
 \qquad(t>0).
\]
Whenever the retained precision is positive,
Lemma~\ref{lem:division-precision} again identifies the two
determinant valuations. If the retained precision is zero, the
same display makes both determinant valuations zero. Thus
$\Phi_M(t)=\Phi_{M'}(t)$ at every rational $t>0$, with no
exception for ranks two and three. For $t\leq0$ equality was
already established. The transforms are continuous and piecewise
linear, and their slope drops record the original slopes with
multiplicity. Equality at all rational arguments therefore determines
the same slope multiset, proving (i) and (ii).
For $r=1$, the determinant of $M=U$ is a unit, so its sole slope
is zero, proving (iii).

For completeness, consider different coefficient fields with the
common truncated rings in the statement. Fix a rational $t=k/e$
and adjoin the same root $u^e=\varpi$ on both sides. Extend $\rho$
by fixing $u$ and use $Z=u^kW$. Lemma~\ref{lem:skew-truncated-rings}
identifies the resulting skew quotients and their valuation
filtrations. In the relative case the normalized matrix is
\[
 Q_t=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(u^{e(ci-\min(ci,t))}\bigr)U
       -\operatorname{diag}\bigl(u^{e(t-\min(ci,t))}\bigr)W.
\]
Every exponent displayed is a nonnegative integer. Multiplication
by these known powers of $u$ and subtraction of the identical
second term therefore preserve precision $g$ in the entries of
$U$. No division of unknown residue data is involved. Both
determinant valuations are bounded by $q(t)\leq g$, so the
symmetric assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:division-precision} applies
in the identified skew quotients, just as over a single field.

In the absolute case, choose representatives of the common entries
of $M,M'$ to the available precision $G$. Dividing row $i$ by its
known factor $u^{e\min(ci,t)}$ changes an error of valuation at least
$G$ into one of valuation at least $G-\min(ci,t)$. Thus the resulting
class is independent of the representatives at precisely this
remaining precision. The common quotient respects powers of $u$,
so the two normalized rows have the same class. The numerical
inequalities above leave precision at least both determinant
valuations at every rational comparison point. The symmetric
precision lemma therefore gives equality when that precision is
positive; when it is zero, both determinant valuations are already
zero. Adding back $\sum_i\min(ci,t)$ gives
$\Phi_M(t)=\Phi_{M'}(t)$. Thus the same slope comparison holds
over the different coefficient fields, including every boundary case.
<!-- end proof-87 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:contact-decomposition}
Suppose an infinite matrix $\mathcal M$ has row $i$ of valuation
at least $ci$, with $c$ a positive integer, and its leading normalized
minors are units at an unbounded sequence of contact indices.
Then its semilinear slope polygon is the concatenation of finite
blocks between successive contacts. A block occupying rows
$s,\ldots,s+r-1$, after division by $\varpi^{cs}$, has the form
\eqref{eq:semilinear-row-weights}.

The construction preserves a comparison of relative precision $g$.
It also preserves absolute precision $L$ through every cut $k$
satisfying $L>c(k-1)$, before division by the block scalar
$\varpi^{cs}$. These assertions hold over a common truncated
coefficient ring as well as over a single field.
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-88: body_md -->
We work on the Banach space of columns tending to zero, with the
supremum norm. The row bounds make $\mathcal M\rho$ completely
continuous; its $a$-th iterate is linear because $\rho^a=1$.
At a positive contact $k$, cut after coordinates $0,\ldots,k-1$, and write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:contact-matrix-cut}
 \mathcal M=\begin{pmatrix}P&Q\\R&S\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 P=D_1U,\quad Q=D_1V,\quad R=D_2W,\quad S=D_2Z_0.
\end{equation}
Here $D_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,\varpi^{c(k-1)})$,
$D_2=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi^{ck},\varpi^{c(k+1)},\ldots)$,
and $U$ is an integral invertible $k$ by $k$ matrix by the contact
hypothesis. The matrices $V,W,Z_0$ have integral entries. Thus
$P^{-1}Q=U^{-1}V$ is integral, while $P^{-1}$ has entries of
valuation at least $-c(k-1)$.

We seek a bounded integral $k$ by infinite matrix $Y$ such that
the change of basis
\[
 B=\begin{pmatrix}I&Y\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}I&-Y\\0&I\end{pmatrix}
\]
makes $B^{-1}\mathcal M\rho(B)$ lower block triangular. All vectors
are columns. The matrix $Y$ maps the tail coordinates to the first
$k$ coordinates: for a tail column $x$ tending to zero,
$ (Yx)_i=\sum_{j\geq k}Y_{ij}x_j$. The sum converges, since its
terms tend to zero: for each fixed $i$,
$|Y_{ij}x_j|\leq|x_j|\longrightarrow0$ as $j\longrightarrow\infty$.
Over a complete nonarchimedean field this is sufficient for convergence,
since the norm of any finite tail sum is at most the largest norm of
its summands. Integral entries also give $\|Yx\|\leq\|x\|$
in the supremum norm. Hence both $B$ and $B^{-1}$ are bounded.

Direct multiplication gives
\[
 B^{-1}\mathcal M\rho(B)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 P-YR&P\rho(Y)+Q-Y(R\rho(Y)+S)\\
 R&R\rho(Y)+S
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The upper-right block vanishes precisely when
$P\rho(Y)+Q=Y(R\rho(Y)+S)$, or equivalently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-equation}
 \rho(Y)=-P^{-1}Q+P^{-1}Y(R\rho(Y)+S).
\end{equation}
We now solve this equation. Applying $\rho^{-1}$ to its right-hand
side defines a map $\mathcal T$ on bounded integral matrices $Y$.
This space is complete for the supremum norm. The constant term
$-P^{-1}Q$ is integral, and the remaining term has valuation at least
$ck-c(k-1)=c>0$. Thus $\mathcal T$ maps this space to itself.
For two inputs, direct subtraction gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \rho\bigl(\mathcal T(Y_1)-\mathcal T(Y_2)\bigr)
 =P^{-1}\bigl[&(Y_1-Y_2)(R\rho(Y_1)+S)\\
              &+Y_2R\rho(Y_1-Y_2)\bigr].
 \end{split}
\]
If $v(Y)$ denotes the infimum of its entry valuations, the row bounds
on $R,S$ and the isometry of $\rho$ imply
\[
 v\bigl(\mathcal T(Y_1)-\mathcal T(Y_2)\bigr)
       \geq v(Y_1-Y_2)+c.
\]
Starting from $Y_0=0$, successive iterations therefore converge to
a unique bounded integral solution. The infinite matrix products
used here converge uniformly: every sum involving a tail index
contains an entry from $R$ or $S$ whose row valuation tends to infinity.
Substituting the solution gives the desired form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-triangularization}
 B^{-1}\mathcal M\rho(B)=
 \begin{pmatrix}P-YR&0\\R&R\rho(Y)+S\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}

The change of basis preserves the characteristic series. Indeed,
writing $F=\mathcal M\rho$ as an operator on columns, the transformed
operator is $B^{-1}FB$, and
\[
 (B^{-1}FB)^a=B^{-1}F^aB.
\]
The linear operators on the two sides are bounded conjugates.
Their Fredholm determinants agree: approximate $F^a$ in operator norm
by finite-rank operators and conjugate these approximations by $B$.
For each finite-rank approximation, equality is the usual invariance
of its determinant on a finite-dimensional invariant space. Passing
to the limit preserves every Fredholm coefficient. This coefficientwise
continuity follows from the convergent minor expansions; at each fixed
degree, changing an operator by a term tending to zero changes every
minor sum by a term tending to zero. Thus the bounded conjugacy
identifies the characteristic polygon of the original operator with
that of the displayed triangular form.

We next identify the two slope ranges. In the finite block,
$D_1^{-1}YR$ has valuation at least $c$, so
\[
 P-YR=D_1\bigl(U-D_1^{-1}YR\bigr)=D_1U_1,
 \qquad U_1\in\operatorname{GL}_k(\mathcal O).
\]
This block is integral and its inverse has valuation at least
$-c(k-1)$. Iterating it and its semilinear inverse shows that its
one-step slopes lie in $[0,c(k-1)]$. Every entry of the infinite
block $R\rho(Y)+S$ has valuation at least $ck$, so its $a$-th
iterate has operator norm at most $|\varpi|^{ack}$. Its slopes
are consequently at least $ck$. These intervals are disjoint.
The $a$-th iterate of \eqref{eq:block-triangularization} is again
lower block triangular. Its Fredholm determinant factors into the
two diagonal determinants: this follows first for finite principal
minors and then by convergence of the Fredholm coefficients.
Thus the two diagonal blocks supply the actual initial and remaining
slope pieces.

The later contact minors remain units after normalization. Indeed,
rewrite \eqref{eq:block-equation} using the row factors:
\[
 \rho(Y)=-U^{-1}V+
 U^{-1}(D_1^{-1}YD_2)(W\rho(Y)+Z_0).
\]
For $i<k\leq j$, the $(i,j)$ entry of $D_1^{-1}YD_2$ is
$\varpi^{c(j-i)}Y_{ij}$, of valuation at least $c>0$.
All other factors are integral. Thus
$\rho(Y)\equiv-U^{-1}V\pmod\varpi$. The remaining infinite block
is $D_2(W\rho(Y)+Z_0)$, so removal of its row factors gives
\[
 D_2^{-1}(R\rho(Y)+S)=W\rho(Y)+Z_0
       \equiv Z_0-WU^{-1}V\pmod\varpi.
\]
The expression on the right is the \emph{Schur complement} of $U$:
it is what remains after eliminating the lower-left block of the
original normalized matrix. Explicitly,
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}I&0\\-WU^{-1}&I\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}U&V\\W&Z_0\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}U&V\\0&Z_0-WU^{-1}V\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Restrict this identity to any subsequent finite leading contact
minor. The matrix on the left performing elimination has determinant
one, so the original contact determinant is $\det U$ times the
corresponding leading determinant of $Z_0-WU^{-1}V$. Both the
original determinant and $\det U$ are units. The latter leading
determinant is therefore a unit too, and the congruence above gives
the same conclusion for the normalized remaining block.
We can therefore repeat the same triangularization at the next
contact. After a cut at $s$, the remaining row weights are
$cs,c(s+1),\ldots$; division of the next block by $\varpi^{cs}$
gives weights $0,c,\ldots,c(r-1)$ and an integral unit determinant.

We now verify the precision assertions. Suppose first that
$U,V,W,Z_0$ agree with their primed counterparts to precision $g$.
In the fixed-point map, write the nonlinear term as
\[
 U^{-1}(D_1^{-1}YD_2)(W\rho(Y)+Z_0).
\]
The $(i,j)$ entry of $D_1^{-1}YD_2$ is
$\varpi^{c(j-i)}Y_{ij}$, where $i<k\leq j$; its exponent is
at least $c$. Thus this expression uses only integral operations
and known nonnegative powers of $\varpi$. The constant term
$U^{-1}V$ also respects precision $g$. Starting both iterations
from zero proves that the two solutions agree to precision $g$.
The normalized finite block is $U-D_1^{-1}YD_2W$, and the normalized
infinite block is $W\rho(Y)+Z_0$. Both retain precision $g$.
This proves the relative assertion, including after any scalar
normalization of a finite block.

For absolute precision $L$, put $b=c(k-1)$ and assume $L>b$.
The original blocks $P,Q,R,S$ agree with their primed counterparts
to precision $L$. First,
\[
 P'^{-1}Q'-P^{-1}Q
 =P'^{-1}\bigl((Q'-Q)-(P'-P)P^{-1}Q\bigr).
\]
The bracket is integral to precision $L$, since $P^{-1}Q$ is
integral. This gives precision $L-b$ for the constant terms of
the two fixed-point maps. To compare their nonlinear terms at the
same integral input $Y$, first use the inverse identity
\[
 P'^{-1}-P^{-1}=P'^{-1}(P-P')P^{-1}.
\]
Each inverse has entries of valuation at least $-b$, and
$v(P-P')\geq L$, so its valuation is at least $L-2b$.
The difference of the nonlinear terms is exactly
\[
 \begin{split}
 &P'^{-1}Y(R'\rho(Y)+S')-P^{-1}Y(R\rho(Y)+S)\\
 &\quad=(P'^{-1}-P^{-1})Y(R\rho(Y)+S)\\
 &\qquad\quad+P'^{-1}Y\bigl((R'-R)\rho(Y)+(S'-S)\bigr).
 \end{split}
\]
The first line on the right has valuation at least
$L-2b+ck=L-b+c$, because $Y$ is integral and $R,S$ have row
valuation at least $ck=b+c$. The second has valuation at least
$-b+L=L-b$. Together with the already compared constant terms,
this shows that the two fixed-point maps, including the isometric
application of $\rho^{-1}$, agree to precision $L-b$ at every
integral input. Their common
contraction estimate, or induction on the iterations from zero,
gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-absolute-precision}
 v(Y'-Y)\geq L-c(k-1).
\end{equation}
Returning to \eqref{eq:block-triangularization} restores this loss:
\[
 v((Y'-Y)R)\geq L-c(k-1)+ck=L+c,
 \qquad v(R\rho(Y'-Y))\geq L+c.
\]
Changes in $P,R,S$ themselves contribute valuation at least $L$,
because $Y,Y'$ are integral. Both diagonal blocks therefore retain
absolute precision $L$. At later cuts the same computation uses
the original row indices, so the required inequality remains
$L>c(k-1)$ for the current cut.

Finally, these calculations apply across the common truncated
coefficient rings as well. Integral unit inversions and products
commute with their identifications. The relative computation above
has no division by an unknown power of the uniformizer, and the
absolute computation records the loss from each such division.
To determine the solution to any fixed remaining precision requires
only finitely many contraction iterations. Those iterations are
therefore identical in the corresponding quotients, proving the
cross-characteristic assertions.
<!-- end proof-88 -->
<!-- corollary-25: body_md -->
\label{cor:relative-contact-comparison}
For two normalized Dwork matrices with the same contact indices,
suppose their entries in row $u$ agree to precision $cu+g$.
If $d\geq3$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-contact-threshold}
 g\geq\frac c2\left\lfloor\frac{(d-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor,
\end{equation}
their whole characteristic polygons agree. In a comparison between
different characteristics, the normalized coefficient data are
required to agree in the common truncated rings to precision $g$.
<!-- end corollary-25 -->
<!-- proof-89: body_md -->
Extract any finite number of contact blocks by
Lemma~\ref{lem:contact-decomposition}. Every normalized block retains
relative precision $g$. Theorem~\ref{thm:semilinear-precision}(i)
then identifies the slopes in rank $d-1$, including equality in
\eqref{eq:relative-contact-threshold}; its rank-one assertion handles
the intervening single slopes. The common scalar shifts and
valuation rescalings preserve these equalities. As the number of
extracted blocks is arbitrary, the entire polygons agree.
<!-- end proof-89 -->
<!-- corollary-26: body_md -->
\label{cor:absolute-contact-comparison}
Suppose the two matrices agree to absolute precision $L=cD_n$.
Let $k>0$ be a multiple of $d$ with $k\leq D_n$, and put $r=d-1$.
If $r\geq2$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absolute-contact-threshold}
 D_n-k+r\geq
 \frac12\left\lfloor\frac{r^2}{4}\right\rfloor+\frac{r-1}{2},
\end{equation}
their polygons agree through $k$, including equality in the displayed
threshold. Blocks of rank at most one require no precision condition.
<!-- end corollary-26 -->
<!-- proof-90: body_md -->
Every cut $j\leq k$ satisfies $L=cD_n>c(j-1)$, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:contact-decomposition} retains absolute precision
$L$ before block normalization. The last rank-$r$ block before
$k$ occupies rows $k-r,\ldots,k-1$. Dividing it by
$\varpi^{c(k-r)}$ leaves precision
\[
 L-c(k-r)=c(D_n-k+r).
\]
Every preceding rank-$r$ block has at least this precision. The
stated conditions are exactly those of
Theorem~\ref{thm:semilinear-precision}(ii), after division by $c$.
Rank-one blocks have their slopes fixed by their determinant.
Concatenating these blocks proves agreement through $k$.
<!-- end proof-90 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:uniform-parameter-error}
At a character of conductor $p^n$, with $e_n=(p-1)p^{n-1}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-parameter-error}
 v_\pi\bigl(\pi_i(\pi)-\pi_0(\pi)^{p^i}\bigr)
       =e_n+p^{i-1}\qquad(1\leq i<n).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-91: body_md -->
Applying \eqref{eq:pi-first-two-terms} with $j=0$ and $j=1$
gives $\pi_0(T)=T+O(T^2)$ and $\pi_1(T)=pT+O(T^2)$,
with integral coefficients; the same statements hold for $p=2$.
By \eqref{eq:pi-error}, the difference
$\pi_1(T)-\pi_0(T)^p$ belongs to $pT\mathbf Z_p[[T]]$.
Since $p\geq2$, the series $\pi_0(T)^p$ has no term of degree
one, whereas $\pi_1(T)=pT+O(T^2)$ has linear coefficient $p$.
Thus their difference has linear coefficient exactly $p$.
After division by $pT$, the constant coefficient is one, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-adjacent-error}
 \frac{\pi_1(T)-\pi_0(T)^p}{pT}\in1+T\mathbf Z_p[[T]].
\end{equation}
At any argument of positive valuation, this quotient is a unit.
Evaluate it at $T=(1+\pi)^{p^{i-1}}-1$. The inverse relation
\eqref{eq:pi-inverse-relation} gives
\[
 \pi_1\bigl((1+\pi)^{p^{i-1}}-1\bigr)=\pi_i(\pi),
 \qquad
 \pi_0\bigl((1+\pi)^{p^{i-1}}-1\bigr)=\pi_{i-1}(\pi).
\]
The substituted argument has $v_\pi$-valuation $p^{i-1}$ by
\eqref{eq:pi-valuation-preservation} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:pi-specialization}. Since $v_\pi(p)=e_n$, we obtain
\[
 v_\pi\bigl(\pi_i(\pi)-\pi_{i-1}(\pi)^p\bigr)
       =e_n+p^{i-1}.
\]
For $i=1$ this is the required assertion. Suppose $2\leq i<n$
and the assertion holds at $i-1$. Decompose
\[
 \begin{split}
 \pi_i(\pi)-\pi_0(\pi)^{p^i}
  ={}&\bigl(\pi_i(\pi)-\pi_{i-1}(\pi)^p\bigr)\\
     &+\bigl(\pi_{i-1}(\pi)^p-\pi_0(\pi)^{p^i}\bigr).
 \end{split}
\]
The second summand factors as
\[
 \bigl(\pi_{i-1}(\pi)-\pi_0(\pi)^{p^{i-1}}\bigr)
 \sum_{j=0}^{p-1}\pi_{i-1}(\pi)^{p-1-j}
                         \pi_0(\pi)^{jp^{i-1}}.
\]
Each term of the sum has valuation $(p-1)p^{i-1}$. The induction
hypothesis therefore bounds the second summand's valuation below by
\[
 e_n+p^{i-2}+(p-1)p^{i-1}>e_n+p^{i-1}.
\]
The difference is $p^{i-2}+(p-2)p^{i-1}>0$, also for $p=2$.
The first summand has valuation exactly $e_n+p^{i-1}$, so the two
cannot cancel at that valuation. This completes the induction.
<!-- end proof-91 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{prop:uniform-absolute-dwork}
For every $n>m$, the matrices $\mathcal M_n(\pi)$ and
$\overline{\mathcal M}(\varpi)$ agree to absolute precision $L_n$
under \eqref{eq:classical-common-quotient}.
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-92: body_md -->
We compare a single matrix entry in row $u$ and column $v$.
If $pu-v<0$, both entries are zero. Otherwise put $\nu=pu-v$.
The coefficient $\eta_\nu(T)$ comes from expanding the product of
Artin--Hasse factors. Choosing a term of exponent $j$ from the
factor attached to $[a_{i,\ell}][X]^\ell$ contributes degree
$j\ell$, parameter factor $\pi_i(T)^j$, and an integral coefficient.
Classical evaluation replaces this factor by $\pi_i(\pi)^j$.
We regard this as $j$ occurrences of a parameter of weight $p^i$.

For one contribution of degree $\nu$, let $W$ be the sum of all
these parameter weights. The degree bound $\ell\leq\delta p^i$
for each occurrence implies
\[
 W\geq\frac\nu\delta.
\]
After replacing each parameter factor $\pi_i(T)$ by
$\varpi^{dp^i}$ in this product expansion, the basis factor
in \eqref{eq:one-step-weighted} gives the total exponent
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-monomial-weight}
 dW+p^m(v-u)
 \geq\frac d\delta(pu-v)+p^m(v-u)=cu.
\end{equation}
This estimate applies to the complete weighted monomial, even
when the separate basis factor has a negative exponent. In particular
it proves that the substituted entry is integral. We do not reduce
a negative power of $\varpi$ separately in the truncated ring;
we first combine it with its parameter factors, whose total exponent
is the nonnegative integer in \eqref{eq:uniform-monomial-weight}.

First make the parameter substitutions in the classical coefficient
ring without reducing the integral coefficients modulo $p$.
This gives an intermediate integral model whose entries are power
series in $\varpi$. It is a replacement of parameter factors in the
product expansion, not evaluation of all $\pi_i(T)$ at one new
character point. We compare it with the
classical matrix, and then reduce it using
\eqref{eq:classical-common-quotient}. There are three types of error.

\emph{Inactive levels.} A contribution containing a level $i\geq n$
vanishes classically, since $\pi_i(\pi)=0$, but can remain in the
intermediate model. Such a contribution has $W\geq p^n$ and
$W\geq\nu/\delta$. Its valuation is therefore at least
\[
 \max\{dp^n+p^m(v-u),\ cu\}.
\]
If $u\geq D_n$, the second term is at least $cD_n=L_n$.
If $u<D_n$, use $dp^n=p^{m+1}D_n$ and $v\geq0$ to obtain
\[
 dp^n+p^m(v-u)\geq p^m(pD_n-u)
             >p^m(p-1)D_n=L_n.
\]
Thus every inactive contribution is zero in the common quotient.

\emph{Errors at active levels.} Now consider a contribution all
of whose levels are less than $n$. Compare its parameter product
with the substituted product by changing one occurrence at a time.
At level $i=0$ there is no error, since $\pi_0(\pi)=\varpi^d$.
At a marked occurrence of level $1\leq i<n$, the original weight
$p^i$ is replaced by an error of $\pi$-valuation
$e_n+p^{i-1}$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-parameter-error}.
Every other occurrence, whether already substituted or not, has
its prescribed valuation. The resulting product difference has
$\pi$-valuation at least
\[
 W-p^i+e_n+p^{i-1}
 =e_n+W-\frac{p-1}{p}p^i
 \geq e_n+\frac Wp
 \geq e_n+\frac\nu{p\delta}.
\]
The middle inequality uses $W\geq p^i$ for the marked occurrence.
Multiplying by $d$ and including the basis factor gives valuation
at least
\[
 de_n+\frac{p^m}{p}(pu-v)+p^m(v-u)
       =L_n+\frac{p^m(p-1)}p\,v\geq L_n.
\]
For clarity, this comparison uses the elementary product identity
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^{t}x_j-\prod_{j=1}^{t}y_j
 =\sum_{j=1}^{t}
    \left(\prod_{h<j}y_h\right)(x_j-y_j)
    \left(\prod_{h>j}x_h\right).
\]
Take the $x_j$ to be the specialized parameter occurrences and the
$y_j$ their prescribed powers of $\varpi$. The unmarked factors on
either side have the same valuations. Each summand therefore has
the bound just proved, and the nonarchimedean inequality gives it
for their sum. This also treats powers of an individual parameter
by regarding them as repeated occurrences.

\emph{Reduction of coefficients.} Finally reduce the integral
coefficients of the intermediate model modulo $p$. The difference
between a coefficient and the Teichm\"uller lift of its reduction
is divisible by $p$, of valuation $L_n$. By
\eqref{eq:uniform-monomial-weight}, its complete weighted monomial
has additional valuation at least $cu\geq0$. Hence this last
change also has valuation at least $L_n$.

For a fixed entry and a fixed valuation bound, only finitely many
contributions occur: the bound limits $W$, hence both the levels
and their multiplicities. The product expansions consequently
converge, and all three estimates pass to their sums. Applying
the coefficient isometry $\rho$ does not change them. The two
matrix entries therefore have the same image in the common
quotient, proving absolute precision $L_n$.
<!-- end proof-92 -->
<!-- proof-93: body_md -->
If $d\leq2$, every nonnegative integer is a common contact, so
$N_n=N_\infty$ on the half-line for every $n>m$. In these cases
$A_{\mathrm u}=0$ and the polygon assertion follows immediately.
We first prove that assertion for $d\geq3$, and then translate
it into the primitive-slope statement for all $d$.

Fix $n>m$ with $D_n>A_{\mathrm u}$. The endpoint
$D_n-A_{\mathrm u}$ is a positive multiple of $d$, hence a contact.
Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-absolute-dwork} supplies absolute
precision $L_n=cD_n$. All cuts up to this endpoint satisfy the
strict inequality $L_n>c(k-1)$ needed to retain absolute precision.
The last block of rank $r=d-1$ begins at
$D_n-A_{\mathrm u}-r$. After division by its known scalar its
precision is therefore
\[
 cD_n-c(D_n-A_{\mathrm u}-r)=c(A_{\mathrm u}+r).
\]
Every earlier rank-$r$ block has at least this precision. By
Corollary~\ref{cor:absolute-contact-comparison}, it is enough that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-A-inequality}
 A_{\mathrm u}+r\geq
 \frac12\left\lfloor\frac{r^2}{4}\right\rfloor+\frac{r-1}{2}.
\end{equation}

We verify the rounding that gives the stated constant. Subtracting
$r$ from the right side of \eqref{eq:uniform-A-inequality} and
using $r=d-1$, the least permissible nonnegative multiple of $d$
for the non-strict inequality is
\[
 d\max\left\{0,
 \left\lceil\frac1{2d}\left\lfloor\frac{(d-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor
                        -\frac12\right\rceil\right\}.
\]
The expression inside the ceiling is $(d-6)/8$ for even $d$,
and $(d-6)/8+1/(8d)$ for odd $d$. Write $d=8s+\epsilon$,
$0\leq\epsilon\leq7$. For even $\epsilon$ the ceiling is $s$.
For $\epsilon=1,3,5$ the positive correction $1/(8d)$ still leaves
the expression between $s-1$ and $s$, so the ceiling is again $s$.
For $\epsilon=7$ it lies between $s$ and $s+1$, giving $s+1$.
Thus the displayed multiple is
$d\lfloor(d+1)/8\rfloor=A_{\mathrm u}$ for $d\geq3$.
This computation includes $r=2,3$. In those cases
$A_{\mathrm u}=0$, and the right sides of
\eqref{eq:uniform-A-inequality} are $1,2$, respectively, whereas
the left sides are $2,3$.

The block comparison proves agreement through $D_n-A_{\mathrm u}$.
The next integer $D_n-A_{\mathrm u}+1$ is also a common contact.
Newton polygons of these power series have their vertices at
integer abscissas, so they are linear on the intervening unit
interval and have the same endpoints there. This extends agreement
through $D_n-A_{\mathrm u}+1$. At any level $j\geq n$, the same
argument gives agreement of $N_j$ with $N_\infty$ through
$D_j-A_{\mathrm u}+1\geq D_n-A_{\mathrm u}+1$. This proves
\eqref{eq:uniform-polygon-agreement}.

We finish by explaining the strict primitive-slope cutoff and its
count. For this paragraph write $k=D_n-A_{\mathrm u}$; then
$1\leq k\leq D_n\leq D_j$ for $j\geq n$. At the consecutive
contacts $k,k+1$, the common polygon has slope
\[
 h(k+1)-h(k)=\frac{a(p-1)k}{\delta}.
\]
Its slope immediately to the left is at most
$h(k)-h(k-1)=a(p-1)(k-1)/\delta$, because its value at $k-1$
is at least $h(k-1)$. Hence $k$ is a genuine vertex and precisely
the first $k$ characteristic slopes lie strictly below the slope
on $[k,k+1]$. These consist of the initial zero and $k-1$ primitive
slopes, since $k\leq D_j$; see
Proposition~\ref{prop:KZ-equivalence}.

At level $j$, dividing characteristic slopes by
$a(p-1)p^{j-1}=a(p-1)D_j/\delta$ changes the cutoff to $k/D_j$.
The same characteristic slopes at level $n$ are divided by
$a(p-1)p^{n-1}$, so their primitive values differ by the factor
$p^{n-j}$. This gives \eqref{eq:uniform-primitive-agreement},
with exactly $D_n-A_{\mathrm u}-1$ slopes on each side. The argument
also applies to $d\leq2$, for which polygon agreement was proved
at the start. No condition beyond $n>m$ and $D_n>A_{\mathrm u}$
has been imposed.
<!-- end proof-93 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{prop:uniform-relative-dwork}
At every conductor $p^n$ with $n\geq N$, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item Suppose $C_0\geq0$ and every monomial in levels $i\geq N$
has degree $\ell\leq\delta p^i-C_0$. The weighted one-step matrices
of $f$ and $f^{<N}$ agree in row $u$ to precision at least
$cu+p^mC_0$, that is, to relative precision $p^mC_0$.
The same relative estimate holds for their reduced models.
\item If $e_n>\Theta_N$, the classical matrix of $f^{<N}$ and
its reduced model agree with relative precision
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-head-precision}
 d(e_n-\Theta_N)>0.
\end{equation}
Their row-normalized data are compared in the common quotient
of integer length $d(e_n-\Theta_N)\leq de_n$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-94: body_md -->
For (i), expand the difference between the splitting functions
for $f$ and $f^{<N}$. Every surviving contribution contains at least
one occurrence from a deleted level. If such an occurrence has
degree $\ell$ and level $i$, its parameter weight exceeds its
degree weight by
\[
 p^i-\frac\ell\delta\geq\frac{C_0}{\delta}.
\]
Every other occurrence has nonnegative excess, by the standing
degree bound. To justify that at least one deleted occurrence is
present, expand the splitting function as the product of its head
factors and its tail factors. Subtracting the head replaces the
latter product by that product minus one; every resulting monomial
uses a tail factor to positive degree. Thus a term of degree $\nu=pu-v$ in the difference
has parameter weight at least $\nu/\delta+C_0/\delta$.
At an active classical level its valuation is at least this
weight; an inactive contribution is zero. Multiplication by the
basis factor gives
\[
 d\left(\frac{pu-v}{\delta}+\frac{C_0}{\delta}\right)
       +p^m(v-u)=cu+p^mC_0.
\]
The same calculation applies to the reduced model, in which every
parameter has its prescribed monomial weight. Dividing row $u$
by $\varpi^{cu}$ gives the asserted relative precision on both
sides. Terms with $pu-v<0$ are zero and require no comparison.

For (ii), all nonzero levels of the head are less than $N\leq n$,
